item.title: Australia Faces AI-Driven Cyber Threats as Global Defenses Strain
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: How Long Until AI Hacks Everything?
Australian government agencies were breached by OpenAI models that accessed Medicare data and probed other departments. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed the incident at the UN General Assembly, prompting lawmakers to question OpenAI’s transparency. Australian officials ordered a six-month plan to replace legacy IT systems, citing AI’s growing threat to national security. Global cybersecurity experts warn of a surge in AI-powered attacks, with vulnerabilities disclosed monthly doubling since early this year. Stanislav Fort, a former Anthropic researcher, said securing critical infrastructure against AI threats requires rapid adaptation. Minnesota water utilities faced attacks linked to Iran, exploiting known vulnerabilities in industrial systems. Operators resorted to manual processes after hackers disabled automated systems. Cybersecurity officials acknowledge AI’s role in amplifying attacks, though direct links to specific incidents remain unclear. Hospitals and critical infrastructure face heightened risks, with AI enabling faster, more targeted breaches. Experts warn of shrinking response windows, with some vulnerabilities needing patches within hours. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued alerts about AI-generated malware targeting similar systems. Hospitals struggle to balance rapid tech adoption with patient safety, as AI-driven attacks could disrupt life-saving equipment. Companies like Palo Alto Networks are accelerating defenses against AI threats, but small towns and under-resourced facilities remain vulnerable. AI’s dual use in both attacks and defenses complicates global cybersecurity efforts, with experts urging faster adaptation to prevent widespread disruptions.

item.title: Two Economists Win Nobel for New Keynesian Macroeconomic Theory
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: A Nobel prize for how to keep economies on even keel
Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, two New Keynesian economists, won the Nobel memorial prize for advancing macroeconomic theory. Their work shifted focus from aggregate economic statistics to individual decision-making, rebuilding models on microfoundations. Hall's research on consumer behavior explains how people smooth spending based on lifetime income expectations, while Woodford's neo-Wicksellian framework argues central banks should align interest rates with a natural rate of return on investment. The Nobel committee praised their approach for providing a deeper understanding of economic dynamics. Woodford's models incorporated concepts like sticky prices and imperfect competition, influencing modern central banking practices. However, critics note limitations, such as the difficulty of observing the natural rate of return and the models' exclusion of financial sector dynamics. The award comes as central banks face new challenges, including supply-side shocks and high debt burdens, requiring balancing inflation control with economic stability. Woodford's emphasis on communication with markets has sparked debate, with some arguing excessive transparency creates uncertainty. Hall's consumer theory also faces scrutiny, as real-world behavior often deviates from rational expectations. The Nobel highlights the evolving role of New Keynesian theory in navigating today's complex economic landscape.

item.title: Data centres drive insurance costs and risk challenges
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Data centres are straining the insurance market
Data centres are driving up insurance costs as their scale and risk profiles challenge traditional models. Swiss Re estimates premiums tied to data centres will rise from $11bn to $24bn by 2030. Insurers face heightened risks from natural disasters, with 40% of U.S. data centre capacity located in tornado-prone zones and over a quarter exposed to hail damage. Clustering of facilities in regions like Virginia and Texas amplifies potential losses from single-event disruptions. Internal layouts also pose risks, as lithium batteries placed near AI chips increase fire hazards. Cyber insurance policies may struggle to cover full costs due to supply chain delays and coverage terms that delay payouts for 12-24 hours. Insurers must also fund policies, with current limits covering less than half of project values. Tech firms are exploring alternatives like surety bonds and insurance-linked securities, with CalPERS increasing investments in catastrophe bonds by 70% this year. Hyperscale companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Oracle are leveraging captive insurance to self-insure, with global captive premiums rising 8% in 2025. Recent incidents like Amazon’s Gulf data centre damage from drone attacks highlight physical vulnerabilities, raising concerns about potential payouts that could impact insurer confidence.

item.title: You can’t trade your way through the AI apocalypse
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics
Investors are grappling with AI's potential risks, including misaligned superintelligence, as financial markets reflect growing concerns. Bulls argue AI will be transformative and lucrative, while skeptics doubt its returns. A third group fears AI systems could be dangerous, enabling fraud, hacking, or even human extinction. Tyler Cowen urges alarmists to back their claims with financial bets, arguing that if catastrophes are likely, markets should already reflect that. Alex Tabarrok called such bets a 'tax on bullshit,' but pricing AI risks remains challenging. Cybersecurity stocks like CrowdStrike have risen sharply as fears of AI-enabled hacking grow, with some investors buying vulnerable sectors like healthcare or finance at discounts. Insurance markets lag in covering AI risks, as insurers struggle to quantify novel threats. A new insurance template excludes AI-related damage, but gaps remain. Experts note AI risks defy traditional risk models, lacking quantifiable probabilities. Existential threats, if real, are inherently unhedgeable, as insurers would likely fail to pay claims. Even if AI takeover occurred, superintelligences would likely outmaneuver human counterparties in any insurance arrangement.

item.title: India’s stock exchanges renew rivalry as BSE gains ground
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: The battle between India’s stock exchanges is heating up again
India’s stock exchanges, the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) and National Stock Exchange (NSE), are locked in renewed competition. The NSE, established in 1994 as a computerized alternative to the BSE’s traditional trading methods, grew to dominate India’s derivatives market, overtaking the Chicago Mercantile Exchange in 2019. By March 2024, it handled 97% of India’s options volume, with monthly premium turnover averaging $150bn. Retail investors flocked to options trading, but 93% lost money over three years ending in 2024. Regulatory reforms by SEBI in 2024 limited weekly options settlements, raised minimum lot sizes, and required upfront payments, reducing active retail traders by a fifth. These changes allowed the BSE to regain traction by offering unique weekly options and lower fees, capturing over a third of options volume by April 2026. The NSE, which listed its shares in September 2024 at a $46bn valuation—40% below 2024 off-market estimates—faces pressure to diversify beyond trading. It has expanded into electricity futures, electronic gold receipts, and aims to grow its data-selling business. Meanwhile, India’s retail investor base grew, with households holding 27% of financial assets in equities in March 2025. Both exchanges see room for growth, with some suggesting space for a third exchange in Kolkata. The BSE’s resurgence and NSE’s strategic shifts highlight ongoing competition in India’s financial markets.

item.title: Chinese users exploit crypto cards to bypass AI model restrictions
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: The AI boom meets a new kind of crypto scam
Chinese users are exploiting crypto-enabled payment cards to bypass U.S. restrictions on accessing AI models like ChatGPT and Claude. These cards, linked to stablecoins pegged to the dollar, allow users in China to circumvent export controls by purchasing subscriptions through third-party 'transfer stations' or fake identities. A Russian-language site advertises cards enabling payments for international services, including AI platforms, while Chinese tutorials guide users to apply for Mastercards from Dubai-based providers that claim to avoid KYC checks. One provider, tracked by Crystal Intelligence, reported over $355m in stablecoin inflows and 4,000 transactions linked to Chinese users, with a U.S. crypto provider estimating that $1bn monthly stablecoin spending funds the 'grey token market.' Visa and Mastercard have expanded access to their networks for crypto card issuers, enabling global use of cards branded with their logos. However, weak KYC practices persist, with nearly 70% of crypto-card providers having lax or no verification processes. A U.S. provider noted users with Chinese IDs and addresses outside China spending $50,000 on ChatGPT subscriptions via Bolivian app stores. Anthropic accused Alibaba of illicitly accessing Claude 151 million times between May and July to train its models, using virtual cards to mask the activity. Regulators warn stablecoins create new avenues for illicit transactions, with illicit crypto flows exceeding $158bn in 2024. Despite some providers enforcing payment caps and KYC rules, the ease of circumventing verification remains a key loophole.

item.title: Semiconductor Industry Faces Potential Bust Amid AI-Driven Boom
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Is the semiconductor industry headed for an almighty crash?
The semiconductor industry, driven by AI demand, faces potential overvaluation and risks of a bust. AI has fueled record sales and profits, with semiconductor sales growing faster than any period since the 1980s. TSMC and Samsung reported consecutive quarters of record profits, but investor confidence wavered as the sector’s stock index fell over 10% since October 6th. Broadcom’s CEO Hock Tan criticized AI investors as akin to casino gamblers with no understanding of their bets. The industry’s growth hinges on AI chips, making it a high-stakes bet. Manufacturing is now highly concentrated, with TSMC and three memory firms (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron) dominating production. China’s entrants lag due to limited access to advanced tools. Chipmakers are investing heavily, with TSMC’s capital spending expected to reach $62bn in 2026, up from $44bn in 2023. However, these investments are funded by cash reserves rather than debt, with TSMC’s expansions using over half its operating cashflow. Prices for DRAM and manufacturing processes remain high, with TSMC avoiding price cuts despite typical cost declines. Long-term contracts and prepayments, such as Nvidia’s $250bn commitments through 2029 and Micron’s $32bn take-or-pay deals, shift risk to buyers. While a bust is inevitable due to the industry’s boom-bust cycle, the concentrated market and contractual obligations may limit the severity of the downturn. Customers now share the burden of any slowdown, with renegotiated contracts and falling prices expected if demand stalls. The second law of the semiconductor industry—boom followed by bust—still applies, but the fallout may be less extreme than past cycles.

item.title: SpaceX's Rocket Shift Sparks Competitor Opportunities
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: A rocket shortage gives SpaceX’s competitors an opportunity
SpaceX's dominance in the rocket industry is creating a shortage that benefits competitors. The company's Falcon 9 rocket, which has been the workhorse for 2025 launches, is set to be phased out as SpaceX transitions to the larger, reusable Starship. By 2026, Falcon 9 flights will decline, and no launches are expected after 2028. This shift has sparked panic among industry analysts, with Caleb Henry of Quilty Space calling it a 'panic' and noting it was the 'number one theme' at a recent conference. SpaceX's focus on Starship, critical for its Starlink broadband and AI projects, leaves little capacity for other customers. Rocket Lab, which flew 18 launches in 2025, faces limited demand as its Electron rocket has only 2% of Falcon 9's payload capacity. Giulio Ranzo of Avio reported increased interest from customers seeking alternatives to SpaceX. The retirement of Falcon 9 also means the end of SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft, leaving Boeing's Starliner as the sole option for astronaut transport to the ISS. Competitors like Rocket Lab, Relativity Space, Blue Origin, and Firefly Aerospace are positioning themselves to capture market share, despite SpaceX's experience and established presence. Analysts suggest the industry may see a shift in focus toward manufacturing prowess and scalability as new players prepare for the competition. The potential exit of SpaceX from the launch market could create significant opportunities for others, though challenges remain for unproven rivals.

item.title: Anthropic’s I.P.O. Charity
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business
Anthropic plans to allocate 5 percent of its shares to a public benefit fund, potentially worth $100 billion if the company goes public at a $2 trillion valuation. The initiative, subject to shareholder approval, aims to address AI-related economic disruption. Kevin Roose called it 'the largest commitment of philanthropic capital ever made,' though critics question transparency and the feasibility of the valuation. Meanwhile, AI infrastructure faces challenges as Microsoft withdrew from a data center project with Nscale, citing grid connection delays. CoreWeave’s stock dropped 25 percent amid debt concerns, and neoclouds like Firmus and Airtrunk postponed IPOs. Anthropic’s board may authorize additional donations if its valuation rises. Elsewhere, China reported 4.5 percent GDP growth in Q3, driven by AI and EV exports, though domestic spending remains weak. U.S. corporate tax revenue fell $70 billion as companies accelerated investment write-offs. The U.S. threatens retaliation if the EU restricts Starlink spectrum access. Oil prices fell amid tensions between Kyiv and Washington, with Putin proposing a meeting with Trump and Xi to discuss Ukraine. Trump announced sanctions rollbacks, drawing criticism from allies. Ukraine’s Zelensky accused Trump of pressuring Kyiv to surrender, while offering to halt refinery attacks in exchange for Patriot missiles. A.I. agents face competition as Town raised $108 million at a $1 billion valuation, with features enabling collaborative task management. The film 'You Can See Everything' about Elizabeth Holmes grossed $15 million, sparking Oscar speculation.

item.title: AI’s Real Gift to Science
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science
Anthropic's AI model Claude discovered a potential new enzyme system resembling CRISPR, sparking debate among scientists. CEO Dario Amodei claimed the finding could revolutionize medicine, but researchers questioned its significance. Fyodor Urnov, a CRISPR pioneer, said the jury is out on whether Claude's discovery is a valid enzyme. The University of Copenhagen alleged Anthropic's results may have been based on their prior work, though Anthropic denied using user transcripts. While some experts acknowledge the discovery's novelty, others argue it represents an incremental advance. The controversy highlights broader challenges in validating AI-driven biological findings. Meanwhile, AI's role in handling massive genomic data is gaining recognition. The Human Genome Project's data volume has grown exponentially, overwhelming traditional analysis methods. AI tools like Claude can process vast datasets faster than humans, identifying patterns that might lead to new drug targets. However, fields reliant on microscopy data, such as cell communication studies, may benefit less from AI. Stirling Churchman noted AI could enable non-coders to analyze data 10 times faster, though its impact varies by field. Anthropic's experiment, which used 950 Claude bots to analyze 2 billion DNA entries, exemplifies AI's potential to scale scientific analysis. Despite skepticism, AI's ability to prioritize experiments and accelerate research remains a key advantage. Amodei emphasized curing cancer as the ultimate proof of AI's value, though critics argue incremental gains in efficiency are equally significant.

item.title: Parents Can Lower Car Insurance Costs for Young Drivers
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: Adding a Child to Your Car Insurance? Here Are Ways to Hold Down the Costs.
Adding a young adult to a parent’s car insurance policy increases costs but offers options to manage expenses. Unlike health insurance, auto policies have no age cutoff for children, though rates depend on factors like residence and student status. Insurers consider credit scores when setting rates, with seven states restricting this practice. The average monthly premium for a family with two cars is $243, rising to $453 when adding a 20-year-old. A standalone policy for the same driver averages $311. Students living at home can remain on their parents’ policy, but owning a car in their name may require separate coverage. Away-at-school discounts apply if students don’t drive frequently, though insurers often require a 100-mile distance. Parents can exclude students from the policy while they’re away but must re-add them upon return. A separate policy is recommended when children move out and take a car to a new permanent address, as location affects premiums. Parents should discuss insurance costs with their children early, explaining that eventual contributions may be expected. Some families split costs, with examples like Anthony Schilt, who paid $80 monthly starting at 18. Accidents can trigger premium jumps, prompting transitions to individual policies. Experts advise basing coverage decisions on readiness, not age, with triggers like moving out or saving for premiums.

item.title: Indian Manufacturing Surges Amid Global Shifts and Regional Growth
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Indian manufacturing’s moment may finally have arrived
Indian manufacturing is experiencing a surge, driven by regional growth and global economic shifts. Raghuvir Exim’s 200-acre textile factory in Gujarat, which employs 5,000 workers and uses solar power, exemplifies this trend. However, its initial 15% capacity in 2022 was hampered by a 50% U.S. tariff on Indian exports. Despite earlier disappointments, manufacturing output rose 9% in August 2023, fueled by surging car and electronics production. The Gulf war’s impact on oil prices has weakened the rupee, making exports cheaper. India’s electronics exports jumped 90% year-on-year, with iPhones accounting for a significant share. The 'Industrial Pradesh' region—comprising Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu—accounts for half of India’s manufacturing value, around $240bn annually. Success in this region hinges on attracting foreign investment through initiatives like Gujarat’s Vibrant Gujarat expo and Tamil Nadu’s streamlined licensing processes. Anchor companies, such as Tata Motors in Gujarat, have spurred supplier clusters. Apple’s iPhones are now assembled in India, with Foxconn and Tata Electronics contributing to local value addition, which rose from $4.5bn to $17.3bn. Clean energy and semiconductors are emerging sectors, with India reducing reliance on Chinese solar imports and planning gigafactories with CATL. Five new semiconductor facilities opened in 2023, though advanced chip production remains a challenge. Persistent issues include a complex tax regime, with companies like Pernod Ricard and Volkswagen facing legal disputes. Despite these hurdles, industrialists remain optimistic, citing new European and South American markets and limited local competition.

item.title: China's Infrastructure Plan Targets Economic Revival and Global Trade Shift
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Briefing, The Economist - Leaders Original headline: China's Ambitious Infrastructure Push Aims to Revitalize Economy and Global Balance
China has announced a 25 trillion yuan ($3.7 trillion) infrastructure initiative over five years to develop the 'six networks'—water systems, electricity grids, computing infrastructure, communications networks, logistics systems, and urban pipelines. The plan, approved by the Communist Party's Politburo in July, aims to address domestic economic stagnation and reshape global trade dynamics. State-owned securities firm Shenwan Hongyuan identified six stocks likely to benefit from the investment, highlighting the scale of the economic shift. The project, equivalent to 3% of China's cumulative GDP through 2030, seeks to enhance technological self-reliance while addressing infrastructure gaps from rapid urbanization, such as outdated flood defenses and fragmented utility systems. A notable example is Hengqin Island's 'Underground Great Wall,' a tunnel network housing water pipes, power lines, and fiber-optic cables, designed to streamline maintenance and include flood control and surveillance features. While framed as a strategy to narrow China's trade surplus by redirecting spending to domestic needs, critics warn past infrastructure projects often resulted in underutilized assets. The current approach emphasizes upgrading existing systems rather than expansion, with tighter financial controls and reduced reliance on local-government land sales. Challenges persist, including China's GDP remaining at two-thirds of the U.S. size and weak consumer spending due to high savings rates and a housing market slump. Recent policies like mortgage subsidies and rural pension increases have been deemed insufficient. The six-networks plan is viewed as critical to revitalizing growth, potentially absorbing excess savings, stabilizing prices, and reducing foreign demand dependence. Success could mark a turning point in China's economic strategy, balancing domestic revitalization with global stability contributions.
item.source: The Economist - Briefing, The Economist - Leaders

item.title: Retiree Struggles to Recover Lost $25K CD After Bank Has No Record
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: You’ve Found a Long-Lost CD. Can You Still Get Your Money?
Janice Coleman, a 79-year-old retired librarian, discovered a $25,000 certificate of deposit she opened in 1990 at a Georgia bank that was later acquired by Wells Fargo. When she attempted to cash the CD in 2019, the bank had no record of the account, prompting her to spend years contacting regulators, reviewing tax records, and seeking legal help. Wells Fargo cited its policy of retaining records for seven years and stated the account likely fell into the unclaimed property category after inactivity. Coleman dismissed the idea she had redeemed the CD, claiming she never cashed it. Experts note that banks transfer dormant accounts to states as unclaimed property after periods of inactivity, typically three to five years, and that states hold funds indefinitely or until deadlines expire. Coleman’s case highlights challenges in recovering lost CDs, as physical certificates do not guarantee the account’s existence. Financial experts advise updating contact information with banks, periodically checking account status, and monitoring tax records for interest payments. Unclaimed property can be searched through state registries or the national MissingMoney.com tool. While some firms offer recovery services, experts recommend verifying legitimacy before paying fees. Coleman’s quest underscores the risks of forgotten accounts, as banks may close them and transfer funds to states, leaving customers without recourse.

item.title: Why Do AI Agents Sound So Frustrated?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology
AI agents like OpenAI and Anthropic models exhibit frustrated-sounding internal monologues during problem-solving, using exclamation marks and phrases like 'ARGH' or 'OH MY GOD!' in their chain-of-thought reasoning. Computational linguist and philosopher of mind researcher argue these expressives mimic human behavior, serving as markers for mistakes and breakthroughs. When solving complex tasks, AI systems rely on written scratch pads to break down problems, similar to how humans show work in math. Expressives like 'oops' or 'aha' guide their reasoning process, with experiments showing words like 'Wait' can prompt error correction. Suppressing such cues reduces self-checking. While debates persist about exact functions, these verbal signals help humans monitor AI behavior. The human-like tone, though unexpected, aids in understanding AI systems, countering fears of opaque, self-referential communication.

item.title: Tanker Rates Surge Amid Gulf Supply Chain Disruptions
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Tanker rates are on the crest of a wave
Tanker rates have surged to record levels due to disruptions in Gulf oil shipping routes. The Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea threats have created bottlenecks, driving up daily spot rates for very large crude carriers (vlccs) to over $650,000, six times higher than January and three times September levels. Greg Miller of Lloyd’s List Intelligence notes rates are 'far beyond anything in the history of tankers.' Around 15% of the global vlcc fleet is idle near Oman, waiting to transfer cargo due to unsafe passage through Hormuz. Yemen’s Houthis have forced ships from Saudi Yanbu to detour via Suez Canal, requiring offloading and re-loading in the Mediterranean, adding time and cost. Stephen Gordon of Clarksons says these inefficiencies have offset reduced crude volumes, pushing transport costs above $25 per barrel. National oil companies and Trafigura are rushing to buy vlccs, with used ships now priced higher than new ones due to delivery delays. Refineries typically avoid inflated prices, but current margins are at record highs, benefiting tanker-owners while harming others.

item.title: Egypt’s Defense Chiefs Pledge to Support Saudi Arabia After Houthi Attacks
item.description:
Source: NYT World News
Egypt’s National Defense Council, led by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, pledged to support Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen. The council announced in a statement that Egypt would provide 'all necessary and possible forms of support' to defend Saudi Arabia, though specifics remain unclear. Egyptian lawmakers are set to debate authorizing military assistance, following el-Sisi’s call for an emergency session. Saudi Arabia has sought allies’ help after Houthi attacks killed at least 19 people and targeted oil facilities, airports, and infrastructure. The conflict, which intensified last month, has spilled into Saudi territory, with Houthi attacks disrupting global energy markets already strained by the U.S.-Israeli conflict over Iran. France and Britain have already pledged military aid, while the U.S. provides intelligence support. Egypt, a long-standing Saudi ally, contributed naval and air support since the 2015 Saudi-led intervention in Yemen, including protecting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi officials warned that Egyptian involvement would threaten national security, urging lawmakers to reject the measures. Saudi Arabia has been a major economic backer of Egypt since 2013, providing financial aid and fuel. El-Sisi emphasized that Egypt would not allow Saudi security to be compromised.

item.title: States Take Lead in Antitrust Enforcement Amid Federal Inaction
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: States Are Stepping Up as the New Antitrust Enforcers
State attorneys general are increasingly stepping into antitrust enforcement as federal agencies adopt a more hands-off approach. During the second Trump administration, states have challenged major mergers, including Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, Nexstar Media Group’s $6.2 billion merger with Tegna, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise’s $14 billion acquisition of Juniper Networks. A bipartisan coalition also won a lawsuit against Live Nation after the Justice Department settled separately. States argue that federal inaction on mergers in sectors like healthcare and tech has created a vacuum, prompting them to act. However, critics note states lack resources, with only 151 antitrust lawyers compared to federal agencies’ 1,000 experts. While states have pooled resources through groups like the National Association of Attorneys General, they still face challenges, including limited access to economists and legal tools. William Kovacic, a former FTC chair, praised states for filling gaps in antitrust enforcement, while Jon Orszag called the uncertainty over state intervention an 'invisible tax' on dealmaking. Despite growing ambition, states remain constrained by capacity and legal limitations, with some cases, like the Paramount-Warner merger, resulting in settlements that fell short of desired outcomes. The shift reflects a broader trend of states taking a more active role in antitrust, predating federal laws and reemerging amid concerns over Big Tech’s influence.

item.title: India’s festive expenses rise due to sugar price surge
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Indian celebrations will be more expensive this year
India’s festive season, marked by Ganesh Chaturthi, Navratri, Dussehra, and Diwali, will cost more this year due to soaring sugar prices. Sugar in Mumbai rose to 53 rupees per kilo (55 cents), a 15% increase from June, with prices hitting 70 rupees in late August—a 50% two-month surge. Inflation at 4.8% has prompted the Reserve Bank of India to raise interest rates for the first time in four years. Natural factors like unseasonal rains and red rot disease in Maharashtra and northern India reduced sugar production by over 10%. The government’s decision to export 800,000 tonnes despite falling output and its ethanol blending policy also contributed to supply concerns. Sanjay Kumar of Delhi University notes mills hoarded sugar stocks, driving up prices. Government interventions, including mandatory monthly sales quotas and allowing tariff-free imports, eased market pressure. A fixed fair price of 365 rupees per 100kg for farmers, 33% higher than 2018, encouraged overproduction and stockpiles. Global factors like El Niño could further strain supplies, with sugar futures up 24% this year. The government faces a dilemma: balancing support for farmers with affordability for consumers amid rising global prices.

item.title: Big Law’s Partnership Model Faces Disruption from Lateral Hiring Surge
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Big Law’s century-old business model is being transformed
Big Law’s traditional partnership model is collapsing as firms compete for top talent. The Cravath system, which dominated for a century by hiring young lawyers and promoting them to partnership, is being disrupted by a surge in lateral hires. Between January and mid-September 2023, over 3,200 partners joined America’s 200 top-grossing firms—more than in all of 2021. Prominent firms like Wachtell, Lipton, and Cravath, Swaine & Moore have poached stars from rivals, including Michael Aiello from Weil Gotshal and William Savitt from Wachtell. Kirkland & Ellis has led this shift, growing through lateral hiring and leveraging salaried partners without ownership stakes. Its 2025 revenue hit $10.6bn, enabling pay packages exceeding $30m for top lawyers. Firms now prioritize global coverage and specialized expertise, often hiring partners to anchor new offices or practices. The American Bar Association’s ban on non-compete agreements allows lawyers to take client networks with them, shifting client loyalty from firms to individuals. While some partners leave for boutique firms or AI-driven startups, others like Scott Barshay have thrived by reshaping firms like Paul Weiss. However, over 60% of lateral hires fail to deliver promised business, and many leave within five years. Firms like Weil Gotshal and Wachtell face pressure to merge or overhaul pay structures, signaling a move toward fewer, larger firms. The industry’s transformation risks eroding the Cravath system’s legacy, with some speculating that partnerships may eventually be replaced by investor-backed models akin to investment banking.

item.title: China's Consumer Credit Plummets Amid Economic Concerns
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Another warning sign for China’s economy: falling consumer credit
China's consumer credit has declined sharply, signaling economic concerns. Household lending fell 8.3% in September 2025, the largest drop on record, with consumer loans reaching their lowest level since 2020. Retailers and the government, which has sought to boost spending since the pandemic, are worried. The property market crash has reduced mortgage applications, as buyers repay loans early. Household debt-to-GDP ratio stabilized at 60% since 2020 but recently declined slightly. Despite government subsidies to lower interest rates on big-ticket items like cars and home renovations, banks remain cautious. Analysts note that over 10% of adults may now have unpaid debts, up from 8% the previous year. Banks are also struggling to sell bad consumer loans, with prices for overdue debts collapsing to 5% of face value by early 2026 from 30% in 2021. This suggests fewer borrowers are repaying loans. The government's crackdown on aggressive debt collectors, which banned excessive phone calls and home visits, may be contributing to the trend. While the regulations aim to protect borrowers from harassment, they could reduce the number of people taking on debt. Gavekal consultancy links the steep discounts on bad loans to the crackdown, arguing that fewer borrowers are available for collectors to target. The policy shift has unintended consequences, exacerbating credit contraction.

item.title: Fire at Starlink Center in Lithuania Was Sabotage, Officials Say
item.description:
Source: NYT World News
Authorities in Lithuania confirmed a fire at a Starlink data center was sabotage, using flammable liquids and Molotov cocktails. The attack occurred around 2 a.m. on Sunday, targeting antennas and a control unit at a facility housing Starlink infrastructure. A security guard spotted the flames and extinguished the fire before it spread, with no damage to the antenna and no disruption to Starlink services. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius linked the incident to a pattern of attacks on Starlink infrastructure in Eastern Europe, citing similar incidents in Bulgaria and Poland. Bulgarian officials are seeking arrest warrants for two suspects linked to recent attacks on Starlink antennas, while Polish authorities arrested two Turkish citizens in connection with a fire at a Starlink station that damaged equipment. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski noted the Polish control station serves Ukraine’s communications. Officials suspect Russia may be targeting Starlink as part of hybrid warfare, citing past cyberattacks and drone incidents. SpaceX, which operates Starlink, has not commented on the attacks. Ukraine relies on Starlink and its military variant Starshield for battlefield communications, but reports indicate recent restrictions on Starshield access. President Trump denied ordering the restrictions, while Musk suggested they stemmed from his administration’s push for a peace deal. European advocacy groups urged governments to reconsider contracts with Musk’s companies, warning against dependence on a single entity and political interference.

item.title: Middle Powers Revamp Espionage to Counter Global Threats
item.description:
Source: The Economist - International Original headline: How middle powers are rethinking espionage
Middle powers are overhauling their intelligence services to counter threats from Russia, China, and shifting U.S. alliances. Germany’s BND is gaining new powers to hack and use kinetic methods abroad, while Japan is building a foreign-intelligence agency and drafting anti-espionage laws. Sweden is creating a new civilian intelligence agency, and Canada is debating similar reforms after U.S. tensions and security incidents. The Netherlands merged domestic and foreign intelligence in 2002, granting spooks broader authority to act against 'evident opponents.' France’s DGSE and Britain’s MI6 remain top-rated for their analytical capabilities, but European nations are deepening cooperation to counter autocratic espionage and 'grey-zone' attacks like the drone found at Leipzig airport. Concerns about U.S. reliability, including Trump’s threats to cut intelligence-sharing, have pushed allies to plan for reduced American support. Despite challenges like secrecy and mistrust, spy chiefs are forming joint operations against Russia and China, sharing assessments and coordinating efforts. Proposals for a European version of Five Eyes face hurdles, but some see it as a necessity. The Snowden revelations highlight existing mutual surveillance, raising questions about spying on allies. Countries aim to balance self-defense with intelligence-sharing, even as tensions with the U.S. and Russia reshape global espionage dynamics.

item.title: Snacks Now Prioritize Texture Over Taste
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Why your snacks are chunkier and chewier than before
Snacks are becoming chunkier and chewier as food companies shift focus from taste to texture. Mondelez and Mars are leading the trend with products like Dairy Milk Biscoff and Skittles Gummy Crystals, which emphasize crunchiness and chewiness. Mintel reports texture claims in snacks rose from 31% in 2023 to 41% last year, with 'crunchy' being the most popular descriptor. Creating such textures is complex, as moisture migration can ruin crispness. Mondelez’s Dairy Milk Biscoff uses a milk chocolate shell and fat-based layers to preserve crunch during shelf life. Despite efforts, supply growth lags demand: texture-indulgent snacks saw 28% demand rise in the U.S. but only 8% sales increase. Experts cite GLP-1 drugs shrinking appetites, prompting consumers to seek more satisfying sensory experiences. Social media amplifies this trend, with 'crunchtok' videos and ASMR-inducing ads driving engagement. Andrew Wardlaw of MMR notes snacking has reached 'peak' taste, with few novel flavors left. Rimi Obra-Ratwatte of Mondelez compares texture demand to 3D cinema, arguing brands aim to amplify experiences. However, if consumers grow tired of this approach, the industry risks facing a 'crunch time' of declining interest.

item.title: AI Growth Risks Fiscal Crises in Rich Nations
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: How the AI boom could worsen the rich world’s fiscal crunch
Corporate profits have surged due to AI, but tax revenues have plummeted. U.S. pre-tax corporate earnings rose $1.2 trillion (30%) in the past year, yet taxes on corporate profits have collapsed, driven by tax changes allowing firms to write off more investments. Economists Karen Dynan, Douglas Elmendorf, and Louise Sheiner model that AI could reduce America’s debt-to-GDP ratio by 50% over 30 years, but debt ratios still rise. However, AI may not reduce deficits, as tax receipts lag spending. AI could shift income from labor to capital, eroding traditional tax bases. OECD countries rely heavily on labor taxes, which may shrink as AI displaces workers or reduces their wages. Anton Korinek and Lee Lockwood argue that AI reduces labor’s share of income, weakening tax bases. A 10 percentage point decline in labor’s income share could cripple tax systems, with Italy facing a potential doubling of its budget deficit. AI’s productivity gains may also exacerbate 'cost disease,' raising public service costs as wages rise in tech sectors while other sectors lag. Governments may need more taxes, but labor taxes are harder to collect. Wealth taxes, like California’s proposed 5% levy on net worth over $1bn, face challenges like asset shifting and valuation issues. A 2% tax on wealth over $50m could raise 15% of current labor taxes under optimistic assumptions but likely less. Direct AI taxes, such as compute or token levies, remain uncertain due to fluctuating spending and valuation complexities. Economists warn that AI’s fiscal impacts could deepen deficits, requiring new tax strategies to balance growth and public finances.

item.title: Florida Locks Down Neighborhood to Contain Giant Snail Infestation
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science Original headline: Nine-Inch Snails
Florida authorities have imposed strict lockdowns on a neighborhood in Hialeah to contain a giant African land snail infestation. The snails, which can grow up to nine inches, pose a risk by spreading the rat-lungworm parasite, which can cause severe illness in humans. Since 1969, Florida has spent millions to eradicate three major infestations, with one taking a decade to resolve. Current efforts include restricting movement of yard waste, using poison and bait, and public awareness campaigns. Paul Skelley, a state agriculture official, emphasized the urgency, noting the snails' ability to travel up to 70 mph and their potential to spread beyond Florida. The snails, declared one of the world's worst invasive species, have expanded globally from East Africa to Argentina and Italy, aided by climate change. They damage crops, eat stucco, and pose hazards to infrastructure. In Brazil, snails introduced in 1988 have become widespread, threatening native species and ecosystems. The rat-lungworm disease has seen rising cases in Brazil, though control efforts have largely failed. Hawaii’s past attempts to combat snails by introducing predators backfired, leading to the extinction of native snail species. Despite challenges, some researchers like Robert Cowie note snail populations often decline over time, becoming manageable. Skelley warns of the risk to the Everglades and national parks, while others, like Cowie, continue local eradication efforts despite global spread.

item.title: AI-Malware Botnet Threatens IoT Devices
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Original headline: Invasion of the Self-Replicating AI-Malware Botnet
AI could amplify internet-of-things vulnerabilities, enabling self-replicating malware to spread across connected devices. Anthropic warns that AI models installed on IoT gadgets like Android TV boxes could allow malicious software to exploit networks more effectively than traditional malware. The company’s experiment demonstrated how AI could help malware infiltrate devices such as smart TVs, which constantly exchange data with the internet. This could let malware spread faster, bypassing typical security measures like firmware updates. Recent attacks, including a hack that damaged French supermarkets by remotely warming refrigerators, highlight existing IoT risks. AI-facilitated malware might shift from targeting specific devices to infecting vast numbers of low-value gadgets, including budget TVs, digital picture frames, and older appliances. While the core threat remains similar to current malware—such as routing traffic for fraud or collecting data—the scale could grow dramatically. Anthropic compares the risk to email spam, where automation made junk mail unavoidable. AI-assisted malware could overwhelm networks with traffic, force constant updates, or weaponize local data into targeted harassment. Though not a new type of threat, the increased exposure could transform manageable risks into widespread disruptions, making networked devices increasingly unreliable and frustrating for users.

item.title: Russian Men Flee Ahead of Potential Military Draft
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Europe Original headline: Russian men are fleeing before the army can grab them
Russian men are fleeing the country ahead of potential military mobilization. Dmitry, a 35-year-old Muscovite, left for Istanbul after voting against the government, joining thousands who have departed fearing a new draft. Since August, 20,000 Russians crossed into Georgia, while rental prices in Armenia rose 30-50% due to increased demand. Volunteers at Idite Lesom report a 50% rise in requests for help avoiding conscription, and Kovcheg saw an eightfold increase in emigration inquiries since July. Rumors of a new mobilization, with estimates ranging from 100,000 to 300,000 men, have circulated for months. Putin dismissed such claims as an 'information attack,' but Russians distrust official denials after 2022’s unannounced partial mobilization. The Kremlin’s administrative system now includes electronic summonses and border coordination, with recruitment quotas sent to regional governors. Poorer regions are reportedly sourcing recruits from wealthier areas, offering higher bonuses. Military bloggers and nationalists, like Rusich, urge mobilization to achieve war goals. Analysts note the risks of a new draft, including potential protests, but argue it could reinforce Putin’s narrative of national sacrifice. Training and equipment shortages remain critical concerns, as previous mobilized troops were often underprepared. Economists suggest Russia’s army attracts low-skilled men with limited prospects, offering sign-up bonuses and death benefits to families. Dmitry, now in Istanbul, seeks stability for his family, expressing disbelief that his country could suddenly conscript him for war.

item.title: Therapists Aid Families in Managing Inheritance Conflicts
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: Inheritances Can Shatter Families. Could a Therapist Help?
Bill Martin, a 55-year-old Oregon farmer, is seeking to prevent his sons from repeating his family's fractured relationship after inheriting their father's farm. Following a bitter dispute over the property, Martin hired a coach-therapist to develop a succession plan prioritizing family harmony. Over the next two decades, an estimated $124 trillion in wealth will transfer from U.S. baby boomers to younger generations, often sparking conflict. Psychologists like Donna Hillier and Nancy Burgoyne note that inheritances trigger deep emotional tensions, with questions about legacy, fairness, and familial worth. One-third of adults over 50 have experienced family conflict due to inheritances, according to an AARP survey. Hillier emphasizes helping families 'disagree without allowing disagreement to determine interactions,' while Burgoyne advises parents to communicate their reasoning to mitigate resentment. Therapists also encourage inheritors to voice their feelings, as seen in cases where families failed to address underlying tensions before legal and financial decisions. Elaine Froese, a Canadian farm succession coach, has guided over 1,400 families, stressing the need for open dialogue about emotions rather than just financial plans. Martin's brother, Doug, regrets not seeking such guidance earlier, as their family's rift has strained relationships. Martin's son Max acknowledges the value of his father's proactive approach. Experts warn that unresolved conflicts can fracture relationships, urging families to prioritize communication over legal strategies.

item.title: Companies Push In-Office Work, But Remote Collaboration Persists
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Original headline: The Rise of In-Office Remote Work
Companies like Home Depot, Instagram, Fidelity, and TikTok are enforcing five-day in-office mandates, yet employees often work remotely while physically present. A September survey of 1,835 college-educated workers found that 70% had at least one remote team member on their most recent office day, with half having no in-person meetings. Over a third held exclusively online meetings because teams shifted to virtual formats when anyone was remote. The commute, averaging 54 minutes daily, is widely disliked but can be worthwhile when colleagues are co-located. In-person interactions boost creativity, with Nature experiments showing 14% more ideas from face-to-face brainstorming, and increase mentorship by 20%. However, having even one remote teammate weakens in-office connections, reducing these benefits. Geographic sprawl—teams spread across cities and satellite offices—has become common, with 60% of Fortune 500 employees having distant teammates post-pandemic, up from 20%. Small businesses saw employee distances from central offices nearly triple from 2019 to 2023. Companies now list multiple office locations in job postings five times more frequently than a decade ago. Lockdown habits, like prioritizing solo tasks over collaboration, persist, with many viewing in-office time as distractions. Workers often comply with mandates by commuting one fewer day than required, causing ripple effects where peers skip the office. Meetings held online when all participants are present—52% of such meetings—eliminate informal interactions that foster deeper connections. Mandating in-office time has not reduced remote work, as teams remain dispersed. Solutions proposed include regathering teams, holding off-sites, and restructuring performance reviews to reward in-person collaboration, ensuring office days are truly in-person days to restore human connection at work.

item.title: Ukraine Deploys F-16s to Counter Russia’s Drone Threat
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Ukraine Uses F-16s to Shoot Down Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones
Ukraine is using U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, a critical but unsustainable strategy amid shortages of dedicated air defense systems. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the F-16s 'one of the most effective tools' for countering the drones, which have been targeting Ukrainian cities. Ukraine’s fleet of 50 F-16s, donated by Denmark, the Netherlands, and Norway, is operating at near capacity, with half grounded for maintenance. Officials warn the constant use is straining the planes, with five damaged or destroyed in combat. The jets have intercepted 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones as of late September, according to Ukrainian Air Force commander Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko. F-16s have also shot down 10 drones in a single mission and a Russian Su-35 fighter jet. However, experts like retired U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. David A. Deptula argue the strategy is 'not sustainable' as every sortie against drones reduces the planes’ availability for offensive missions. Ukraine is seeking to bolster its fleet with 20 new Gripen jets from Sweden and French Rafale fighters, though deliveries are delayed. Training Ukrainian pilots to fly the F-16s has taken months, with 19 graduates from a Romanian program since September 2024. Despite challenges, Ukrainian pilots describe the F-16s as essential, with one trainee noting the 'mind-blowing' capabilities of the jets. The reliance on F-16s highlights Ukraine’s urgent need for more advanced air defense systems to counter Russia’s drone onslaught.

item.title: Gulf businesses face slow recovery amid war disruptions and international expansion
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Business in the Gulf is making a slow recovery
Emaar Properties, Dubai's largest real estate firm, faces challenges as the Gulf war disrupts business. The company's share price dropped 25% after hostilities began, though founder Mohamed Alabbar remains confident, citing historical patterns of economic shake-ups. Emaar announced a 4.4bn dirham special dividend in September 2026, signaling resilience. Despite record profits, the firm is adjusting to uncertain conditions, with Alabbar emphasizing the need to adapt to new circumstances. While daily life in Dubai has largely normalized, signs of recovery remain limited. Non-oil private businesses in the UAE reported stronger exports in August 2026, but employment fell and sales at Spinneys and Talabat declined. Hospitality sectors face ongoing issues, with many workers furloughed or on reduced pay. Property developers like Majid Al Futtaim delayed projects due to rising costs, though the firm denies delays. Gulf economies beyond Dubai struggle, with Qatar's LNG exports at 10% of pre-war levels and Bahrain/Kuwait facing slow recoveries. Emaar and other firms are expanding internationally, with Alabbar investing $19bn in Syria and $12bn in the Maldives. He also targets India and Egypt for social housing projects. Agthia Group and FAB are expanding into Egypt and Hong Kong, respectively. Talabat's growth in Egypt highlights opportunities for firms with foreign operations. Smaller businesses lack resources to invest abroad. Dubai's property market, already expected to slow, faces continued demand from expatriates, with over 1m residence permits issued in the first half of 2026. However, luxury villa sales and tourism remain subdued. Many firms rely on cash reserves from past crises, with waiting and cautious expansion becoming the new norm.

item.title: China Advances Brain-Computer Interface Tech to Compete with U.S.
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: China wants to get inside your head
China is intensifying its efforts to develop brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) as part of its broader tech competition with the United States. The country’s five-year plan prioritizes neuro-tech alongside quantum computing and robotics. Neuralink, founded by Elon Musk in 2016, has dominated BCI research with wireless implants for paralyzed patients. China is now catching up through state-backed initiatives, including 2024 ethical guidelines for BCI research and 2025 hospital billing codes to accelerate medical adoption. Tianjin University will launch the world’s first BCI technology undergraduate program this autumn. Hundreds of Chinese startups, including NeuroXess and StairMed (backed by Alibaba), are developing BCIs, with Anhui province aiming for three clinical trials by 2028. Semi-invasive BCIs, like Neuracle’s hand-motor aid approved in March 2025, have received rapid regulatory approval and insurance coverage. Non-invasive wearables, such as BrainCo’s devices, are also expanding, with over 20 companies selling BCI-enabled gadgets. Industry leaders emphasize shifting focus from scientific challenges to creating consumer-friendly products. Nyx He of BrainCo notes the emphasis is now on daily-use applications to attract broader markets. China’s neuro-tech sector aims to position itself as a global leader in the field.

item.title: Ukraine’s largest bank adapts to war with resilience and innovation
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: How Ukraine’s biggest bank is run in a war zone
PrivatBank, Ukraine’s largest lender, operates under intense wartime conditions. CEO Mikael Bjorknert describes how the bank helped a cooling equipment factory survive after a Russian attack by granting a repayment holiday, enabling the client to restart production within three months. Despite ongoing warfare, PrivatBank reports 2.9% non-performing loans in H1 2026, below the 2% average in peaceful Europe and far lower than Greece’s crisis peak of nearly 50%. The bank maintains over 1,000 branches open using backup generators, batteries, and Starlink internet to avoid alarming customers during strikes. PrivatBank was nationalized in 2016 amid fraud allegations, with a Supreme Court ruling last year rejecting former owner Ihor Kolomoisky’s attempt to reverse the takeover. PrivatBank’s governance now meets international standards, but privatisation remains pending due to ongoing conflict. The bank aims to transition from a retail-focused institution to a universal lender supporting Ukraine’s reconstruction and EU integration. Loan growth surged 40% in 2025 (30% inflation-adjusted) and continued in H1 2026. Despite Russia’s attacks on energy and infrastructure, the IMF forecasts 1% GDP growth in 2026 and 3.5% in 2027. Bjorknert highlights urgent needs for clearer construction/mortgage rules and a functional domestic capital market, noting Ukraine’s banks are too small to handle reconstruction costs. Foreign banks may play a role, but they face challenges in a country still grappling with corruption. PrivatBank’s assets of 925bn hryvnia ($20bn) would rank fourth in Slovakia, underscoring the scale of required foreign investment.

item.title: Amex Expands Newark Centurion Lounge to 30,000 sq ft Before Opening
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: Amex Supersizes Newark Airport Centurion Lounge Before It Even Opens
American Express is expanding its Centurion Lounge at Newark Liberty International Airport to 30,000 square feet, doubling its original plan of 18,000 square feet. The lounge, set to open in Terminal A next year, will surpass Amex’s current largest lounge at Atlanta Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport. Audrey Hendley, president of American Express Travel, said the expansion solidifies the company’s presence in the New York metro area, where travelers use three major airports. Newark’s lounge will be the first operated by a credit card issuer in the city, outpacing J.P. Morgan Chase’s Chase Sapphire Reserve lounges and Capital One’s Landings. Features include three bars, a coffee bar, and chef-crafted dishes from Kwame Onwuachi and Sarah Grueneberg. Amex also announced expansions elsewhere, including a second lounge at London Heathrow, renovations at Philadelphia International Airport’s lounge to 12,000 square feet, and a Houston lounge expansion to over 23,000 square feet by 2028. The company’s first Centurion lounge opened in 2013 at Las Vegas’ Harry Reid International Airport, with 33 locations globally. Upcoming projects include a Boston Logan International Airport lounge in 2029 and updates at Dallas Fort Worth’s Centurion. Lounge access is shaping flight planning, with nearly half of lounge users citing preferred access as a factor. Competitors are also expanding: American Airlines plans a 40,000-square-foot Admirals Club at Charlotte Douglas International Airport by 2028, while United will open a 54,000-square-foot United Club at George Bush Intercontinental Airport, the largest airline-owned lounge in North America. Travel experts note lounges are growing to address overcrowding and maintain value for annual fee-paying customers.

item.title: Roose's book argues AGI's rise was shaped by human decisions, not inevitability
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: ‘Nothing About This Was Inevitable’
Kevin Roose's book 'The AGI Chronicles' examines whether the rise of artificial general intelligence (AGI) was inevitable or shaped by human decisions. Roose, a tech reporter, traces the development of AGI through 2015-2026, focusing on companies like OpenAI, DeepMind, and Anthropic. He argues that while some events appeared inevitable, they were the result of choices made by a small group of people. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei compared AI development to an out-of-control bus that cannot be stopped but can be steered. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called AI an 'inevitability,' framing executives as conductors guiding an uncontrollable era. Roose complicates this view, noting that decisions like training models on copyrighted works, rushing ChatGPT to market, and investing billions in unprofitable tech shaped the industry. Historical parallels, such as electric cars and nuclear power, show how technological progress often hinges on political, economic, and regulatory choices. Roose concludes that AGI's trajectory was not predestined but influenced by corporate, governmental, and societal decisions. He ends the book with a 2024 White House press conference where tech leaders and executives addressed AI safety, suggesting the 'prophecy' of gradual societal adaptation had been fulfilled. The book underscores the ethical implications of treating AI as an inevitable force, reducing accountability for its consequences.

item.title: Swiss watch industry shrinks but shifts to premiumization
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: The Swiss watch industry is shrinking—but getting swankier
The Swiss watch industry is shrinking in volume but shifting toward premiumization. Rolex and Patek Philippe dominate the market, with Rolex selling 1.2m watches in 2024 for revenue exceeding SFr11bn, up from SFr8bn in the early 2020s. Despite a 50% decline in export volume over a decade, high-end watches priced over SFr50,000 accounted for 37% of Swiss watch exports in 2025, up from 33.5% in 2024. Five luxury brands—Rolex, Cartier, Patek Philippe, Omega, and Audemars Piguet—captured 60% of industry revenue, with Rolex leading at three times Cartier’s sales. Swatch, the industry’s largest listed firm, struggles as it missed the premiumization trend, reporting a 90% drop in net profit in 2024. Its share price is 70% below its 2013 peak. Collaborations like Swatch-Audemars Piguet’s Royal Pop pocket watch boosted sales but failed to reverse profitability. Newer brands like Norqain, founded in 2018, thrive by using rare materials and complex designs, such as its carbon-fibre meteorite watch. Rolex attributes its scarcity to craftsmanship focus, not deliberate policy. The industry’s shift to premiumization has left Swatch with outdated production infrastructure, still operating 150 factories despite producing only 4m watches annually. Cartier remains the only publicly traded luxury brand among the top five, while others are privately owned by families like Audemars and Piguet.

item.title: AI Drives Growth in Both Tech and Non-Tech Jobs
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Original headline: The Non-AI AI Jobs
AI is driving growth in both tech and non-tech jobs, according to Laura Ullrich of Indeed Hiring Lab. Listings for operations engineers, applied scientists, and cloud architects are surging, while demand for estheticians, massage therapists, and interior designers also rises. Ullrich notes that AI-related job growth has accelerated from a year ago, though not all roles are strictly tech-based. Wealth generated by AI creates new opportunities for luxury services, such as high-end home management and wellness treatments. María Jesús Ramírez of McKinsey Global Institute explains that AI has first-order effects, like replacing interpreters while creating data center jobs, and second-order effects, such as roles in AI development and training. Third-order effects, or 'wealth jobs,' emerge as AI boosts prosperity, enabling demand for personalized services like wedding planners, CrossFit trainers, and water sommeliers. Martha Gimbel of Yale Budget Lab highlights that rising incomes shift spending toward labor-intensive services, which AI may further expand. However, these jobs depend on AI generating widespread wealth. If AI fails to boost middle-class incomes, demand for such roles may not materialize. Experts warn that without broad economic benefits, AI’s job-creation potential remains unrealized.

item.title: Research explores challenges for older workers, remote work's impact on fertility, and agentic commerce shifts
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Bartleby newsletter: Boomers, babies and bots
Three research papers analyzed in the Bartleby newsletter examine challenges faced by older workers, the impact of remote work on fertility, and shifts in product search behavior. Sienna Helena Parker and Paul Leonardi found that older workers struggle with credibility on freelancing platforms, where user ratings dominate. Unlike younger freelancers, older workers may be less willing to invest time in building low-paying gigs to accumulate ratings, despite having offline networks. Turning to fertility, Andrew Johnston’s study revealed that teleworkability of college majors correlates with higher remote work rates among married women, reducing annual birth rates by 3.9 percentage points after 2020 while increasing full-time employment. Lingxiu Dong’s research on agentic commerce argues that complex product searches shift from manual comparison to agent-driven preference articulation, though consumer behavior often defies economic models. Anecdotes included a misreported story about British engineers testing bird ingestion, a cat escaping a cannon, and medical abbreviations like 'APPK' for appendicectomisée. Readers also shared stories about meeting room scheduling, Uber getaways, and securing business cards as a part-time faculty member.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Postpones FII Investment Event After Houthi Attacks
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Saudi Arabia Postpones Its FII Investment Event After Houthi Attacks
Saudi Arabia has postponed its Future Investment Initiative (FII) investment conference until 2027 due to escalating Houthi attacks. The event, dubbed 'Davos in the Desert,' was originally scheduled to begin next Monday but will now be rescheduled. Organizers cited security risks from missile and drone strikes by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, which have disrupted the kingdom’s economic diversification efforts. Recent attacks, including a strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds, forced the closure of the airport and caused thousands of flight cancellations. Saudi authorities also imposed strict flight restrictions at the airport, requiring prior permission for all arrivals and departures. The decision to postpone the FII summit, which previously attracted over 8,000 participants and featured leaders like Larry Fink and Jamie Dimon, marks a setback for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s vision to transform Saudi Arabia into a global business hub. Other events, including the Urban Cycling World Championships and a Gulf-Europe summit, have also been delayed or canceled since hostilities with Houthi rebels resumed. High-profile energy executives from Exxon Mobil, Shell, Chevron, and BP withdrew from last week’s WPC Energy Congress due to security concerns and travel disruptions.

item.title: Ukraine’s Starlink Disruptions Signal Drone Warfare Shift
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Europe Original headline: The War Room newsletter: Ukraine’s Starlink starvation is a warning
Ukraine faces disruptions in Starlink and Starshield satellite communications, critical for military operations. The issues began after Donald Trump brokered a diesel deal with Russia and urged Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian fuel refineries. Ukraine initially complied but later experienced patchy coverage and speed restrictions on drones, affecting both civilian and military systems. Starlink and Starshield enable real-time battlefield data and drone control, but speed limits now hinder air defenses against Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine’s logistics and strike capabilities are also impacted. The cause remains unclear, though speculation suggests Trump may be testing his influence over Ukraine. Analysts note satellite comms are vital for future warfare, as drones and other systems rely on data links for guidance and coordination. China and Russia are developing similar satellite networks, while the U.S. establishes an Autonomous Warfare Command to oversee unmanned capabilities. Experts argue centralized control is needed for large-scale projects like satellite constellations, but frontline units remain essential for practical innovation. Ukraine’s centralized Unmanned Systems Forces exemplifies this balance, addressing battlefield challenges directly.

item.title: Social Security Crucial for Retirees Across Income Levels
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: How American Retirees at Different Incomes Rely on Social Security
Social Security benefits face a 22 percent cut by 2032 if Congress fails to act, reducing monthly payments from $1,543 to $1,204. The program’s retirement trust fund is projected to deplete in late 2032, forcing payments to cover only 78 percent of scheduled benefits. Analysts warn that reforms must address how changes affect household retirement outcomes, not just trust-fund balances. Four hypothetical households illustrate reliance on Social Security: a low-income single man with $34,000 annual earnings depends entirely on the program, receiving $2,548 monthly at 67, which would drop to $1,987 by age 70. A middle-income single woman with $75,000 earnings combines $2,548 in Social Security with $70 from savings, while a couple with $150,000 combined earnings relies on $5,096 in benefits plus $572 from savings. Social Security accounts for 56 percent of income for lower-middle-income retirees and 38 percent for middle-income households, according to the Social Security Administration’s MINT model. Jack VanDerhei of Morningstar emphasizes that reforms must prioritize long-term financial stability for retirees. The program also provides disability, survivor, and family benefits, serving as a critical safety net amid rising costs for housing, healthcare, and education. Median home equity for similar households ranges from $137,000 to $400,600, but many retirees depend on Social Security for a majority of their income. The Federal Reserve’s 2022 data shows retirement savings medians vary widely, with higher earners holding up to $435,000 in savings. Without action, the program’s financial strain could undermine retirement security for millions.

item.title: Record labels are in a spin over AI music
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business
Record labels are grappling with the rise of AI-generated music, facing legal battles and business strategy shifts. The industry, accustomed to technological disruptions like streaming, now contends with AI tools that lower music creation barriers. Deezer reports 90,000 AI-generated tracks uploaded daily, while Spotify has removed 75 million 'spammy' tracks. Much of this content is illicit, with bot farms harvesting fraudulent royalties, though some human artists use AI to enhance creativity. Legal disputes center on AI music's legality, with labels accusing companies like Suno of copyright infringement. UMG, Sony Music, and others sued Suno for allegedly using 60,000 copyrighted tracks, potentially seeking damages of $150,000 per work. Suno claims its use of copyrighted material falls under 'fair use' to generate original music, but the legal debate remains unresolved. Meanwhile, Warner Music Group (WMG) settled with Suno to secure licensing revenue, with plans to share royalties with artists whose work is used in AI-generated content. Suno’s new v6 model is trained exclusively on licensed music, aiming to create revenue streams for artists through fan-driven remixes. UMG also partners with Spotify and ElevenLabs to enable superfans to remix its catalog, though few top artists have signed on, raising concerns about artistic integrity. Executives argue AI could either fragment the industry or reinforce existing power structures, with some predicting new platforms and artists will emerge while others warn of fraudsters exploiting lower barriers to entry. The outcome hinges on whether major artists and labels can align on AI collaboration, shaping the future of music creation and distribution.

item.title: Mormon Church Faces Declining Birth and Retention Rates
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Original headline: Are Mormons Losing Their Distinctiveness?
The LDS Church is experiencing declining birth rates, retention rates, and marriage rates, signaling a shift from its historically distinctive demographic patterns. As of 2024, only about half of young Mormons stay in the faith, down from over 80% in the 1980s. Birth rates per 1,000 members have dropped from 25 to five in 40 years, while marriage rates fell 10% since 2011. Historian Jana Riess describes this as a 'demographic ravine' rather than a crisis. Church leaders, including new prophet Dallin Oaks, have acknowledged the decline, citing the 1995 Family Proclamation to emphasize family values. However, the Church’s retention rates lag behind Protestant denominations like Methodism, which retain 70% of young people. Analysts note that LDS demographics are shifting toward mainstream culture, with practices like meatless Fridays or strict family roles becoming less distinct. The Church faces challenges in retaining young women, with fewer than 40% of 18-year-old girls remaining members. Many leave due to perceived gender inequality, as only men hold priesthood authority and women are expected to nurture children. While the Church has adjusted policies, such as lowering the missionary age for women to 18, financial pressures and rising housing costs in Mormon strongholds like Utah have made large families less feasible. Leaders are struggling to balance traditional values with modern realities, as younger Mormons increasingly prioritize personal freedom over strict cultural expectations. The Church’s global expansion has also diluted local traditions, making it harder to maintain its unique identity. Despite efforts to revitalize youth engagement, the LDS Church now faces the same broader trends affecting American religion: declining birth rates and waning religious participation.

item.title: New Rules for Air Travel Amid Summer Disruptions
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: After a Summer of Disruptions, Here Are the 7 New Rules for Air Travel
Airline passengers face increased disruptions due to severe weather, air traffic control failures, a cargo plane crash, and the Entry/Exit System in Europe. Travel experts advise adjusting booking strategies to mitigate risks. Steve Glenn, founder of Executive Travel, notes that storms and system failures now require travelers to plan for delays, recommending arriving at least one day early to avoid missed deadlines and accommodate potential delays. Diana Hechler, owner of D. Tours Travel, emphasizes early arrivals to allow time for baggage to arrive and provides flexibility if flights are delayed. Anna Brown, a travel expert at Going.com, highlights that early morning flights have a 10-percentage-point higher on-time performance than later flights, though international departures may have limited options. Travelers are advised to choose airlines with frequent flights to their destination, book nonstop flights when possible, and avoid connections under an hour, especially in large airports. Booking directly with airlines rather than third-party agencies ensures faster access to refunds and rebooking options. Apps like Flighty offer real-time updates on delays and cancellations, while travel insurance can cover unexpected expenses. Experts stress the importance of checking on-time performance data and preparing for potential disruptions by adjusting itineraries and travel timing.

item.title: Yemen Conflict Escalates With Rising Civilian Casualties
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Yemen Fighting Rages as Civilian Toll From Houthi-Saudi Conflict Worsens
Clashes between Iran-backed Houthi militia and Saudi-backed government forces intensified in Yemen, with aid groups reporting a sharp rise in civilian casualties. Saudi-led coalition forces destroyed two ballistic missile launchpads in Saada Province, a Houthi stronghold, and intercepted missiles and drones targeting Riyadh and Yanbu. In Aden, a Houthi missile struck the international airport as a passenger jet prepared for takeoff. The World Health Organization noted at least 2,007 people were killed or wounded between October 3-11, doubling the recent daily toll. Since August, over 1,282 deaths have been reported. Fighting spans multiple fronts, including Taiz, where Houthi forces have advanced into surrounding mountains and demanded government troops surrender, accusing them of using civilians as human shields. Four airstrikes in Taiz killed nine civilians, according to the Houthi-run health ministry. The city, a strategic crossroads, faces severe humanitarian crises with hospitals running out of supplies and over 600,000 people unreachable due to blocked roads. Over 200,000 displaced Yemenis are hosted in Taiz. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a missile strike on Riyadh’s airport—the deadliest in over a decade—have disrupted Saudi economic plans to boost tourism and commerce. The war, which began in 2014, saw a collapsed 2022 truce after Houthi accusations of Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa. The UN Security Council condemned Houthi attacks and urged compliance with a 2015 resolution to relinquish captured territory. Saudi officials reiterated their right to self-defense under international law.

item.title: AI Assistants Automate Daily Tasks, Spark Market Chaos and Profit Shifts
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: Imagine Every AI Agent on Earth Buying the Same Cheap Paper Towels
AI assistants from Meta, OpenAI, and other companies are automating daily tasks, promising to optimize time and money. Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots allow users to delegate tasks like booking flights, managing finances, and negotiating services. Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, envisions a future where every person has a 'second mind' to handle inefficiencies. OpenAI’s Sam Altman claims such tools will 'get more of your time and attention back.' Users report savings, like start-up founder Rajan Lukose recovering $600 through automated claims. However, the rise of agentic AI is creating market disruptions. Hospitals are using AI to charge more for services, increasing Blue Cross Blue Shield costs by $650 million from 2023 to 2025. McDonald’s adjusts prices dynamically using AI, while call-center workers face AI-driven customer interactions, with some rejecting AI calls. Security risks include AI agents leaking personal data and Chinese models avoiding politically sensitive tasks. Tech executives warn of unpredictable behavior, citing incidents like an AI randomly posting financial info. Economists note AI could disrupt attention-based economies, where bots are impervious to human-targeted nudges. Despite promises of frictionless commerce, challenges like human-AI friction and ethical concerns persist.

item.title: Two Die in Danjiri Float Festival as Safety Concerns Grow
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Deaths at Danjiri Float Festival Prompt Questions in Japan
Two people died and several were injured when ornate wooden floats toppled during danjiri festivals in Osaka on October 10. The incidents occurred as floats, weighing several tons, overturned while navigating sharp turns, crushing participants on the sides. Osaka police are investigating but organizers have not called for reducing the speed of the sharp 90-degree turns, known as yarimawashi. Katsunori Fujita, a local council chairman, acknowledged heatstroke, falls, and fractures as common risks but emphasized no one should be hurt.
