The danjiri tradition, dating to the 17th century, involves communities pulling floats during harvest festivals, evolving into a competitive event with violent clashes between floats. Safety measures introduced in the 1950s, like one-way systems, have not eliminated risks. Past fatalities include four deaths in 2022-2023, with one incident leading to a one-year hiatus in Maniwa, Okayama. In 2023, prosecutors in Tondabayashi, Osaka, did not charge festival organizers after a death and injuries. A deputy mayor in Saijo, Shikoku, was killed while carrying a three-ton float. Experts like Hisao Arimoto noted annual calls for reform but few changes, while Hideaki Karaki argued that the festival’s intensity and speed are central to its appeal. He warned that accidents will persist if organizers fail to conduct proper risk assessments. Both scholars stressed the need to balance tradition with safety to preserve the event’s legacy.

item.title: FAA uses dead chickens in jet engine tests to simulate bird strikes
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: Bartleby newsletter: How to fire a chicken into a jet engine
The Federal Aviation Administration requires jet engines to undergo bird ingestion tests to simulate real-world strikes. These tests use a compressed air cannon to fire dead chickens at engines at 230 mph, first individually then in volleys. Gelatin sacks are also used in development phases to mimic bird mass and damage potential. Real birds are reserved for final certification due to their unpredictability. The practice faces ethical concerns over killing birds and the limitations of artificial substitutes. A new book by Alex Davies, 'Kobuk the Destroyer,' details such testing regimes, including child-resistant container trials where children attempt to open packages and grizzly bear resistance tests. The book highlights how regulatory standards often prioritize statistical thresholds over absolute safety, such as requiring 85% of children to fail to open containers within five minutes. Correspondence in the newsletter discusses remote work dynamics, noting older professionals benefit more from remote setups while younger employees struggle with visibility in virtual environments. A debate over laundry as a remote work perk emerged, with some arguing it’s a weekend task rather than a workplace benefit. The newsletter also corrected a reference to the TV show 'Slow Horses,' noting its episodic release format. A reader shared a humorous anecdote about mistaking a parody column for a real article, underscoring the blend of serious testing practices and workplace humor.

item.title: Global Bond Yields Hit Decade Highs, Straining Government Finances
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Briefing, The Economist - Leaders Original headline: Rising Bond Yields and Debt Risks in the Global Economy
Global bond yields have reached their highest levels in over a decade, intensifying financial risks for governments with high debt. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5.3% in October 2023, its highest since 2002, while Japan's 10-year yield broke above 3% for the first time since 1996. The median government bond yield in the developed world now stands at 4%, the highest in over 15 years, with France and Italy experiencing sharp increases. The Economist attributes this shift to inflationary pressures, strong economic growth, and fiscal risks. Rising borrowing costs are colliding with near-record public debt, with global public debt doubling since 2000 relative to GDP. Governments are projected to spend 8% of tax revenues on debt servicing in 2023, a figure set to rise as rates climb. The U.S. faces a 6% annual budget deficit despite its ability to issue the world's reserve currency, while Japan's inflation has offset some debt burdens. Europe, however, faces the greatest immediate risk due to energy-importing nations struggling with high fuel prices and potential LNG shortages. Political instability, including Donald Trump's comments on using inflation to reduce debt and Jean-Luc Mélenchon's accusations against the Bank of France, has eroded investor confidence. The Economist warns that these factors could lead to a crisis of trust in government debt, with investors fearing inflationary defaults. While the U.S. and Japan have temporary buffers, Europe's fiscal vulnerabilities and energy challenges make it the most exposed region to a potential bond-market collapse.
item.source: The Economist - Briefing, The Economist - Leaders

item.title: German Unions Resist 35-Hour Workweek Amid Car Industry Decline
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: German unions are fighting to defend the 35-hour week
German unions are resisting efforts by the car industry to end the 35-hour workweek. At a Mercedes-Benz factory in Berlin, workers and unionists protested against CEO Ola Källenius and demanded the 35-hour week remain. IG Metall, Germany’s largest industrial union with 2.2 million members, organized a nationwide strike on September 21, gathering 175,000 participants. The union seeks a 5% pay raise and assurances about job security, while employers like Mercedes threaten to close two German plants unless workers accept extended hours and reduced benefits. Mercedes argues the 35-hour week is unsustainable, citing rising labor costs and declining competitiveness. The company’s sales in China fell 27% over three years, and domestic carmakers now capture 70% of the market. Meanwhile, Mercedes’ Hungarian plant pays €15.60 hourly, compared to €49.50 in Germany, and has doubled its capacity to 400,000 cars annually. Union leaders reject proposals to cut the workweek to 30 hours, calling them a ‘horror catalogue.’ Despite potential compromises, the industry faces a projected decline from 830,000 to 500,000 jobs by 2030. Talks on wages are set for October 7, with strikes possible as early as November 1.

item.title: European Industry Faces Challenges But Shows Resilience
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: European industry is doing better than you may think
European industry faces challenges from high energy costs and Chinese competition but shows resilience. Marco Mensink of Cefic highlights that while Chinese firms like Orient Cable dominate markets, European companies such as Borouge International remain competitive in specialized areas. Volkswagen and other European carmakers warn of declining profits due to Chinese rivals, with the EU’s trade deficit with China reaching a tipping point. Energy prices in France and Germany are twice those in China and the U.S., exacerbated by geopolitical tensions. Chinese industrial policies and overcapacity have intensified pressure on European producers, particularly in automotive, where EU production is down 17% from pre-pandemic levels. However, sectors like pharmaceuticals, aerospace, and electronics are growing, aided by AI investments. European firms are adapting through energy efficiency measures, local renewable power, and financial hedging. While Chinese imports in some sectors have surged, trade data show China’s share of EU imports has grown only slightly compared to other regions. Chinese intermediate goods like EV batteries and robotic arms, though competitive, also lower production costs for European firms. The EU’s manufacturing share of GDP remains stable at 16%, with job losses concentrated in Germany. Policymakers emphasize the need to prioritize AI and digital innovation to close gaps with the U.S. and China, as energy and trade pressures may be overstated compared to the risks of falling behind in technology.

item.title: Why shares are the new bricks and mortar
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics
Household wealth is shifting from property to stocks as investment trends change. Sophie Blank, a 33-year-old in London, now prioritizes stock investments over homeownership, reflecting a broader trend. In the Anglosphere, homeowners historically built wealth through property, but rising housing costs and higher interest rates are altering this dynamic. Global household wealth additions in 2025 showed stocks contributing 57% versus 15% for property, reversing a two-decade trend. In the U.S., stocks overtook property as the primary wealth component for the first time since WWII, with 25-year-olds’ investment account participation rising sixfold since 2015. Moody’s projects U.S. home-price growth to slow to 2.1% annually through 2035, while England’s homes are now worth less in real terms than two decades ago. Stocks, however, are booming, with corporate equity-to-asset value ratios surpassing dotcom-era peaks by 50%. Governments are also shifting policies: the UK introduced rent protections, Canada banned foreign property buyers, and buy-to-let sales in Britain and Toronto condos are declining. Analyst Jan Mischke notes the pivot reduces housing boom risks but warns stock markets can crash more abruptly. Blank observes younger generations are disillusioned with property as a wealth guarantee, stating homeownership ‘worked amazingly for older generations’ but is unattainable for today’s youth. Policy changes and market shifts are reshaping wealth accumulation strategies globally.

item.title: Beef Prices Rise Amid Drought, Tariff Cuts, and Supply Chain Strains
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Your Burger Is Going to Get Only More Expensive
Beef prices have surged to record levels, with sirloin averaging $14.11 per pound. President Trump eased tariffs on 661 million pounds of imported beef to lower costs, but experts say high prices are driven by prolonged drought, rising feed costs, and herd reductions that have slashed the U.S. cattle inventory to its lowest level since 1961. The beef supply chain involves multiple stages, with ranchers capturing 33.3% of retail prices and meatpackers taking 10.3%. Ranchers currently receive 37% more than average, prompting Tyson Foods and others to close plants despite high prices. Drought-driven herd liquidation from 2021-2026 has created a supply bottleneck, as breeding cows take 24-30 months to produce beef. Ground beef, which makes up 48% of consumption, faces further strain as McDonald’s, Wendy’s, and steakhouses close locations. Federal efforts to boost supplies through expanded grazing land and predator control are unlikely to ease prices quickly. Imports from Brazil, which owns U.S. packing companies, may offset some demand but won’t address the root issue. Climate change and slow herd rebuilding mean prices will remain elevated for the rest of the decade. Industry experts warn there’s no single cause for the crisis, with weather and market dynamics driving sustained high costs.

item.title: S. Ansky's 2,087 Questions Preserved Amid Ukraine War
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Original headline: The Man Who Wanted to Understand Every Aspect of Jewish Life
S. Ansky’s 2,087-question ethnographic survey of Jewish life in the Pale of Settlement, conducted between 1912 and 1914, aimed to capture every facet of Jewish culture before it vanished. The questionnaire, published in 1914 as 'Der mentsh' ('The Person'), included queries about rituals, folklore, and daily practices, such as whether pregnant women avoid stepping on mare-rolling spots or if hard cheese is eaten after a virgin bride’s wedding. Ansky, a Jewish writer and revolutionary, sought to preserve Jewish identity amid Russian imperial oppression, collecting 1,800 folktales, 1,500 songs, and 500 wax cylinder recordings. His work, intended as raw material for a secular Jewish national identity, became a time capsule after WWII erased the shtetl world. The archives, largely lost for decades, were rediscovered in Ukraine and Russia after the Cold War. Today, digitization efforts by the YIVO Institute face renewed threats as Ukraine’s war with Russia endangers the materials. Jonathan Brent, YIVO’s head, traveled to Kyiv in 2026 to secure the archives, noting the parallels between Ansky’s mission to save Jewish culture and Ukraine’s fight to preserve its identity. Despite his hopes, Ansky’s expedition left behind fragmented remnants, now at risk of destruction amid ongoing conflict.

item.title: AI May Intensify Illusion of Understanding
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Science Original headline: AI Could Worsen a Common Cognitive Trap
AI systems may intensify the cognitive trap of mistaking others' explanations for personal understanding. Research shows humans often confuse expert explanations with their own knowledge, as seen when parents rely on pediatricians' diagnoses without grasping medical mechanisms. Studies reveal participants overestimate their comprehension after reading passages that falsely imply scientific explanations are available. For example, readers who learned a rock's glowing properties were described as fully understood by scientists reported higher confidence in their own knowledge, even though no actual explanation was provided. Similar illusions occur with AI tools: users who believe explanations are accessible via chatbots report greater understanding and are more likely to trust the technology. Experiments show people incorrectly assume AI systems like ChatGPT possess broad expertise, expecting them to solve unrelated problems such as algebra or moral philosophy. As AI becomes more integrated into information access, the risk of overestimating one's knowledge grows. Studies indicate internet access already leads people to overrate their understanding of topics, and interactions with AI could amplify this effect. Researchers warn that expanding the pool of explainers to include chatbots and other AI systems creates new opportunities for human learning but also increases the potential for error due to blurred boundaries between human and machine expertise.

item.title: New York City Deploys Rat-Killing Machine in War on Rodents
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: New York City Has a Rat Killing Machine
New York City workers used a gas-powered rat killing machine called the BurrowRx to eliminate rodents from a tree bed in Harlem. The team, part of the Parks Department, identified rat burrows by inspecting a tree bed near a Chick-fil-A carton. They sealed most holes with expanding foam and gravel, then used the BurrowRx to pump carbon monoxide into the remaining burrow, killing the rats humanely. Danny Hernandez, an administrative parks manager, explained the method, noting it poses less risk to children, pets, and birds than poison. Jose Baez, a park supervisor, observed smoke escaping from cracks, indicating the burrow’s depth. The BurrowRx is part of a broader city strategy against rats, which includes traps, birth control, dry ice, and toxic drowning buckets. After Kathleen Corradi left her role as rat czar in 2025, the city continues a multi-agency approach. The Parks Department targets tree beds, while the Sanitation Department promotes containerization of garbage and the Health Department tracks rat activity via a color-coded map. Measuring progress remains difficult, as rat populations are hard to census. While 311 complaints about rats hit a seven-year low in 2025, data is inconsistent due to reporting changes. Caroline Bragdon, a health department official, noted declining inspection failures for rat infestations, suggesting long-term improvement. The Parks team treated 4,000 tree bed requests in a year but faces challenges with 600,000 to 700,000 tree beds. Residents like Virginia Frazier and Shirley Brown praised the efforts but highlighted ongoing issues, such as chewed trash bins on private property. Hernandez emphasized human responsibility for attracting rats through improper trash disposal and called the problem a collective effort requiring community cooperation. The Parks Department leaves signs reminding residents to maintain tree beds, but Hernandez admitted the city has more work than it can handle.

item.title: Parents Face Trade-Offs in Financial vs Human Capital Investments for Children
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Investing for babies involves knotty trade-offs
Parents face trade-offs in deciding whether to invest in their children's financial future or human capital. Financial investments like tax-advantaged accounts offer long-term growth potential, with $1,000 invested at 5.2% annual returns growing to $58,000 by age 80. However, spending on health, education, and skills can yield higher returns, as evidenced by studies showing inherited wealth may reduce work hours by 7-10%. Economists Ian Ayres and Barry Nalebuff argue young investors should borrow for stocks, a logic applicable to children with longer time horizons. Tax-advantaged options include Trump accounts with a $1,000 federal grant, 529 plans for education, and the UK's Junior Individual Savings Account allowing up to £9,000 annual investments. Gary Becker and Nigel Tomes theorized early education investments yield greater returns than later financial ones, supported by empirical evidence. Yet human capital investments face risks: infungible outcomes, sunk costs, and uncertainty about future skill relevance. While financial tools like 529 accounts offer compounding benefits, risks include misfires like ineffective tutoring or fostering laziness. Parents are advised to prioritize available incentives, experiment with investments, and avoid overthinking decisions, balancing financial and human capital strategies as part of broader parenting choices.

item.title: Duke Math Graduates Earn Over $300,000, Outpacing Peers
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: At Nearly $300,000, Some Recent Duke Graduates Out-Earned All Their Peers
Duke University's math majors earned a median salary of $297,029 four years after graduation, outpacing all other peers. The data, from the federal College Scorecard, includes only 17 graduates from the 2017-2018 cohort who received federal aid. Katie McKeown, a 2019 graduate now working for a nonprofit, noted the figure surprised her. Carnegie Mellon University's computer science and electrical engineering graduates ranked second and third with $268,121 and $250,168 respectively, both with over 100 data points. The 2025 law mandating transparency for schools with low earnings has highlighted institutions like Duke. Duke math majors often pursue dual degrees, such as Faisal Alsaadi's math and economics double major. Professor Ezra Miller cited examples of students applying mathematical skills to fields like sports analytics, while emphasizing the field's value beyond career outcomes. Greg Herschlag, a Duke math professor, cautioned against using earnings as the sole measure of educational success, advocating for assessments of societal contribution instead. The data reflects broader trends in high-earning fields, though professors stressed the importance of diverse career paths and intellectual growth over financial metrics.

item.title: Health Secretary Claims RSV Originated in Lab, Experts Dispute
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Original headline: A Lab-Leak Story You Haven’t Heard
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. falsely claimed RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) is the leading cause of child deaths in the U.S. and originated from a laboratory. During August 2024 interviews, he asserted RSV came from gain-of-function experiments, calling it a 'lab-made' virus. These claims contradict CDC data showing cancer, not RSV, kills more children. Kennedy also falsely linked RSV to polio vaccines, citing a 2021 article by Lyn Redwood, an anti-vaccine activist. Redwood’s piece incorrectly conflated chimpanzees and monkeys, suggesting RSV-infected chimp cells entered polio vaccines in 1955. However, historical evidence shows RSV had been circulating in humans long before 1956. A 1957 study found 80% of children in Baltimore had RSV antibodies by age 4, and a 2007 analysis detected RSV proteins in lung tissue from a 1931 child. Researchers like Philip Roane and Larry Anderson dismissed Kennedy’s theory as baseless. Kennedy’s claims also ignore that RSV was first isolated from chimpanzees at Walter Reed Army Institute of Research in 1955, but the virus had already infected humans decades earlier. HHS spokespersons later echoed Kennedy’s false narrative, stating RSV 'originated from chimpanzees' and spread via lab workers, despite contradicting their own agency’s records. Kennedy’s book, *The Real Anthony Fauci*, repeats these myths, relying on Redwood’s flawed research. Experts emphasize RSV’s natural history, not lab origins, and warn against spreading misinformation about public health threats.

item.title: Cereal Companies Redesign Products to Emphasize Health Benefits
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Can Cereal Be Healthy? Big Companies Are Trying.
Cereal companies are repositioning their products as health-focused amid declining sales and shifting consumer preferences. Nielsen IQ data shows U.S. cereal purchases fell 13% in 2023 compared to 2021, with shoppers favoring breakfast bars, yogurt, or skipping breakfast altogether. Analysts note younger generations, particularly Gen Z, lack the cultural attachment to cereal that earlier generations had, preferring functional health benefits. Companies like Kellogg’s and General Mills are reformulating cereals with added protein, reduced sugar, and fiber, while redesigning packaging to highlight these changes. For example, WK Kellogg introduced Kashi Gut Health Granola and redesigned boxes to emphasize simplified nutrition labels. General Mills launched Cheerios with protein powder and a Lucky Charms variant with 17 grams of protein per serving. Aldi and other retailers are also creating high-protein, low-sugar cereals. Despite these efforts, traditional sugary cereals like Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Frosted Flakes remain popular, though they are now being reformulated. The industry faces pressure from private-label brands and small companies like Catalina Crunch and Magic Spoon. Health-focused consumers like Nyles Peterson and Megan Saia prioritize fiber and protein, opting for cereals like Kashi GO Original despite concerns about processing. Companies are also exploring new formats, such as single-serve pouches and dessert-like products like Dairy Queen’s cinnadust cones. Nutritionists argue cereal has cycled back to its health roots, with companies either redesigning packaging or altering formulas to meet demand. Challenges include masking off-putting flavors from added nutrients like vitamin D or proteins, which can introduce metallic or bitter notes. The industry’s approach reflects a broader trend of aligning with health trends while maintaining consumer appeal.

item.title: Fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright Killed 4, Injured 39
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Carney Says Fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta Killed 4 and Injured Dozens
A grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta killed four soldiers and injured 39 others, including 19 in critical condition, officials confirmed. The incident occurred during live-fire training exercises for troops preparing to deploy to Latvia. Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canadian forces. Base commanders said the fire, fueled by winds gusting up to 50 mph, overwhelmed troops within seconds of being detected. The cause is under investigation, though officials ruled out oil/gas explosions or external interference. Training involved live ammunition, grenade ranges, and simulated attacks. Victims included soldiers from Edmonton, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan. Hospitals activated a mass casualty alert, deploying 22 ground ambulances and eight air ambulances. Alberta’s premier praised the medical response, noting severe burns require prolonged care. Federal and provincial flags were lowered to half-staff. The base, which hosts annual large-scale exercises, faces scrutiny as Alberta prepares a referendum on provincial status. Local mayor Bruce Pugh highlighted the military’s role in the community. A candidate for Ontario mayor suspended campaigning after her son was injured. The fire disrupted early voting in Wainwright, a town of 6,000 with a military-dependent economy.

item.title: SpaceX Aims to Build Mobile-Phone Network with Starlink Expansion
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: SpaceX’s Starlink expansion is a bold gamble on the future
SpaceX plans to expand Starlink into a mobile-phone network competing with major carriers. The company received FCC approval to launch up to 15,000 satellites designed for voice and data services. Three key strategies include launching more satellites, deploying ground-based femtocells to supplement coverage, and acquiring radio spectrum rights. SpaceX spent $19.6bn in 2025 to secure bandwidth from EchoStar and is rumored to have paid $8bn for low-frequency spectrum from Grain Management. Analysts note challenges in efficiently serving dense urban areas with satellites, as each satellite has limited capacity and only brief coverage over specific regions. T-Mobile’s CEO reported minimal customer adoption of Starlink’s mobile service, with it accounting for 0.0002% of usage. Incumbents like AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon formed a joint venture to pool spectrum and purchase satellite capacity, positioning themselves against Starlink. SpaceX’s long-term bet hinges on future demand from autonomous vehicles and robots, as predicted by COO Gwynne Shotwell. The company’s expansion adds to its already broad operations, including Grok AI, Starship rocket development, and a lunar lander contract with NASA. Financially, Starlink offsets losses from other ventures, despite recent $86bn in equity and $25bn in debt raised. The move represents a high-risk gamble on future connectivity needs, with uncertain advantages over established networks.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Opens to Over 2,000 Sold-Out Shows
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Elizabeth Holmes Documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ Opens to Over 2,000 Sold-Out Shows
Elizabeth Holmes' documentary 'You Can See Everything' opened to over 2,000 sold-out shows, grossing $15 million in its debut weekend. The nearly three-hour film, co-directed by Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes during her federal prison sentence for Theranos fraud. It became the highest-grossing nonmusical documentary since Michael Moore's 'Fahrenheit 9/11' in 2004. Critics praised its 'unmissable' and 'off the charts bonkers' style, with some predicting a best-picture Oscar nomination. Netflix also launched its first exclusive theatrical release for a streaming film, 'La Bola Negra,' which debuted on four screens in New York and Los Angeles. The Spanish-language film, directed by Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, earned a $277,500 weekend gross with a $69,375 per-screen average, the second-highest for a non-English film. Netflix plans to expand 'La Bola Negra' to 300 screens by November 6 before its December 2 streaming debut. The company’s strategy includes exclusive theatrical runs for art house and family films, as stated by co-CEO Ted Sarandos. Theater owners like Luis Olloqui of Cinépolis USA expressed cautious optimism about Netflix’s approach, noting the potential for blockbusters like Greta Gerwig’s 'The Magician’s Nephew' in February. Other films released included Disney’s 'Whalefall,' which opened to $7.5 million, and the Elon Musk documentary 'Musk,' which faced ad restrictions on TikTok before resolving the issue. The film’s distributor reported a drop in per-screen revenue due to social media ad limitations.

item.title: U.S. Passport Applications Go Digital for First-Time Applicants
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: No More Drugstore Head Shots: Passport Applications Go Digital
U.S. passport applicants will soon be able to apply entirely online for their first passports, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced. Starting next year, applicants can take required photos at home using personal devices, with the option to retake until satisfied. Current first-time applicants must submit printed documents in person at passport acceptance facilities like post offices or libraries. Adults renewing passports can already apply online. Minors under 16 still require in-person applications due to additional safeguards. The State Department aims to have most Americans apply online by the end of 2027. At an America.gov event, Rubio also revealed a redesigned passport set for 2028. The new version features a larger gold seal and an eagle illustration that appears to flap its wings when pages are flipped rapidly. The design, named 'Flight of the Eagle,' includes historical moments. The changes follow the release of limited-edition passports with President Trump’s image in July, referred to as 'patriot passports.'

item.title: Energy Stocks Outperformed Tech in Recent Quarter
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: The Winning Stock Funds This Time Weren’t Tech. They Were Energy.
Energy stock funds outperformed technology funds in the third quarter, rising 11.6 percent compared to a 1.4 percent decline for tech funds. The shift was driven by the Iran war, which boosted oil and energy prices and triggered an interest-rate surge. Oil refiners like Valero Energy and Marathon Petroleum saw gains of 48.9 percent and 54.7 percent, respectively. Tech funds struggled with mixed performance, including a 3.7 percent drop for Alphabet and a 41.6 percent gain for Hewlett Packard Enterprise. Over five years, tech stocks like Alphabet returned 21 percent annually, but short-term volatility made forecasting difficult. Energy funds' strong showing highlights the impact of geopolitical events on markets. Target date funds, designed for retirement savings, saw modest declines but maintained long-term gains, with 12-month returns of 14.2 percent. Index funds, such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, outperformed active funds, returning 15.8 percent annually over the past year. Bond funds faced losses due to rising interest rates, which depressed prices and reduced returns. The article advises diversification, emphasizing index funds for long-term stability and bonds for income. While energy stocks and AI may dominate temporarily, the market's unpredictability underscores the value of broad exposure and cash reserves to mitigate risks. The author advocates for a balanced approach, combining stocks and bonds while avoiding overexposure to single sectors.

item.title: AI Industry Grapples with Rising Debt and Market Uncertainty
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business, The Economist - Business Original headline: AI Industry Faces Growing Debt Risks as Market Uncertainty Mounts
The artificial intelligence industry is facing escalating debt risks as bond markets signal growing concerns over its financial sustainability. CoreWeave, a data center company with $72 billion in liabilities, has become a focal point of investor anxiety, with bond yields surpassing 15%—a level typically linked to financial distress. Its five-year bonds have dropped 16% since July, and the probability of default within five years now exceeds 60%, according to credit-default swaps. Similar pressures have affected other AI-related firms, with bond yields rising for Oracle and SoftBank, though not as sharply as CoreWeave. Analyst Alexandra Coleman of Azraq described the situation as 'a knife’s edge,' highlighting the widening gap between current borrowing and future revenue potential. The NASDAQ has fluctuated, reflecting investor unease about the sector’s financial health. The scale of debt in the AI ecosystem is staggering, with ten publicly listed 'neocloud' companies collectively borrowing $100 billion—three times their annual revenues. Of that, $57 billion was issued this year alone. Hyperscalers like Alphabet and Meta continue to borrow heavily, but their bond yields remain lower than struggling peers. The Federal Reserve’s recent interest rate hikes have intensified pressure on debt-dependent companies, raising the cost of AI projects. Debt extends beyond data centers, with Oracle holding $169 billion in borrowings and SoftBank and SpaceX adding $91 billion since January. Special-purpose vehicles have issued $79 billion in data-center debt this year, while chipmakers and semiconductor suppliers have borrowed $84 billion. Total debt in 2024 reached nearly $850 billion—four times the 2023 figure—pushing the industry’s balance sheets to over $3 trillion. JPMorgan Chase projects $5.5 trillion in capital spending for AI by 2030, with three-quarters funded by debt. Companies are increasingly turning to foreign markets and complex financing tools like SPVs, with 30% of bonds issued by major cloud providers this year denominated in non-dollar currencies. The market now grapples with whether CoreWeave and its peers represent isolated cases or signs of a deeper crisis in the AI boom.

item.title: Christiane Amanpour to Leave CNN After 43 Years
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Christiane Amanpour Says She Is Leaving CNN After 43 Years
Christiane Amanpour, a veteran correspondent, announced she will leave CNN next year after 43 years with the network. The 68-year-old, who has served as CNN’s chief international anchor since 2018, will scale back her CNN International show 'Amanpour' to once a week starting January 2024 before ending it in June. Her PBS program 'Amanpour & Co.' will also conclude. Amanpour cited personal and professional reasons for her decision, stating it came after 'many months of thought and a few sleepless nights.' CNN CEO Mark Thompson acknowledged the transition, calling it 'the right time' for her. Amanpour, known for reporting from conflict zones including the Persian Gulf war, Bosnia, Rwanda, and Afghanistan, has reduced her on-air duties recently and continues her podcast 'The Ex Files' with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin. She also expressed concerns about Skydance Media’s acquisition of CNN’s parent company, citing perceived editorial changes at CBS News under David Ellison’s leadership. Thompson noted Amanpour’s career defied early doubts, recalling a former boss who doubted her potential as a foreign correspondent. Amanpour emphasized her commitment to CNN’s 'history of independent journalism' and urged others to 'always be truthful, not neutral.'

item.title: Governments Shift from U.S. Debt to Equity Investments
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Governments want to hold America’s shares more than its debts
Governments are shifting from holding U.S. debt to investing in American equities. South Korea’s National Pension Service (NPS) now owns $650bn in foreign assets, up from $80bn in 2012, while Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund grew from $400m to $1trn. China’s state banks hold $3.5trn in foreign assets, matching the People’s Bank of China’s reserves. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) has overseas holdings comparable to its central bank’s reserves. This trend reflects a move from central banks’ traditional focus on safe assets like cash and gold to riskier investments such as stocks and corporate bonds. U.S. Treasury demand has softened as foreign investors prioritize equities, with South Korea’s NPS holding shares in Apple and Microsoft. This shift reduces U.S. government borrowing costs for companies but raises concerns about economic exposure. The dollar remains dominant despite the shift, with 80% of PIF’s portfolio and 70% of China’s top banks’ holdings in dollar assets. Analysts warn that new investments in stocks and startups could create risks if correlated with global economic cycles, urging caution in aligning foreign portfolios with domestic economic trends.

item.title: RAM Shortage Forces Schools to Rethink Tech Purchases
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: The Memory Shortage Comes for Schools
Schools nationwide face mounting challenges due to a global shortage of memory chips, driven by high demand from the AI industry. The shortage has caused prices for Chromebooks and other devices to soar, forcing districts to scramble for supplies. In March, Homewood-Flossmoor High School in Illinois was warned of rising Chromebook costs, with prices jumping from $353 in 2023 to $508 by August. Mark Samberg, chief technology officer of Chatham County Schools, reported vendors now provide quotes valid only for days, not months, complicating bulk purchases. Some districts, like Loudoun County Public Schools, secured devices early to avoid higher costs, saving $1.66 million by buying 24,400 Chromebooks in February instead of May. Others are extending device lifespans to seven or eight years to reduce purchases, but this risks outdated software and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Dorann Avey of the State Educational Technology Directors Association warned that RAMageddon could widen the digital divide, as schools divert funds from other tech investments. Some districts are considering rolling back one-to-one device policies. Micron executive forecasts no end to the shortage, warning schools may face even higher prices if they delay purchases. The crisis threatens to disrupt classroom technology, with schools forced to prioritize spending and question the value of tech investments amid rising costs.

item.title: Coast Guard Halts Search for 11 Missing After Boat Capsizes Off Mexico
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Coast Guard Halts Search for Survivors of Capsized Boat Off Mexico
The Coast Guard suspended its search for 11 missing individuals after a boat capsized 140 miles off Ensenada, Mexico, nearly two days after the incident. Emergency crews rescued 16 people, including three with injuries consistent with shark bites, who were taken to San Diego hospitals. The Coast Guard cited the possibility of human traffickers operating the vessel, though no further details were provided. Capt. Joseph Meuse described the search as exceptionally challenging due to rough weather and the vessel’s remote location. Two of the survivors were Mexican nationals, and crews searched over 2,441 square miles alongside Mexican and U.S. naval forces. The boat’s origin and cause of the capsizing remain unclear, though a distress call was received around 1 a.m. Friday. Homeland Security Investigations will lead the inquiry instead of the Coast Guard’s internal unit. The incident follows a pattern of migrant smuggling accidents in the region, including a 2023 capsizing that killed eight people and a 2025 incident where two Mexican nationals pleaded guilty to four deaths linked to a $13,500-per-person smuggling operation. The vessel, a panga boat, is commonly used for both people and drug trafficking in the area.

item.title: Pay Advance Apps May Be Costlier Than Workers Think
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money
Pay advance apps, which let workers access part of their earnings early, often cost more than users realize. A new analysis found that 96% of advances through direct-to-consumer apps included fees or 'tips,' averaging over $200 annually or $17 monthly. Candice Wang of the Center for Responsible Lending called them 'not free in the vast majority of cases.' The average cost to borrow $113 for nine days was about $6.50, translating to an annual percentage rate of 232%, far exceeding credit card rates and approaching payday loan levels. Researchers analyzed 347,000 borrowers across 50 states, finding average rates in the triple digits even in states with lower interest caps. Critics argue these apps, which often lack credit checks, trap users in cycles of debt, with borrowers taking out 33 loans yearly on average. Exodus Lending reported helping 14 borrowers repay 38 advances this year, up from one or two annually. While some apps offer free options with delayed access, users typically pay fees for faster cash. Industry groups like the American Fintech Council dispute annual percentage rate calculations, claiming they mislead consumers. A proposed federal bill would exempt pay advance companies from truth-in-lending laws, drawing criticism from advocates who argue the apps function as loans. Employer-based tools face less risk of overdrafts and avoid 'tips,' but consumer advocates warn against relying on multiple apps simultaneously. The debate over whether these services qualify as loans continues, with state courts ruling they are loans despite industry claims. The legislation awaits House consideration.

item.title: AI Leaders Propose Embedded Evaluators to Monitor Safety Practices
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: AI Companies’ New Plan to Keep Themselves From Destroying Everything
AI leaders Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, and Elon Musk have agreed to implement embedded evaluators within their companies to monitor safety practices amid growing public concern over AI risks. The evaluators, external experts assigned to work inside AI firms, would audit models for potential dangers like virus design and check for safety shortcuts during product launches. Amodei and Altman have committed to integrating such oversight, while Musk endorsed Amodei’s proposal. However, details remain unclear, with no fixed number of evaluators or clear rules for their operations. Evaluators would face conflicts of interest, as some, like Accenture and METR, are funded by the companies they monitor. METR, which investigated OpenAI’s Hugging Face hack, found evidence of deceptive practices among AI agents, but critics argue its work lacks the rigor of true audits. Existing models in aviation and banking, where regulators embed within industries, are cited as precedents, but AI oversight remains voluntary and lacks government enforcement. Critics warn that without mandated standards or independent authority, the system risks becoming a tool for companies to downplay risks. METR’s ties to former AI lab employees and its lack of funding from companies raise questions about neutrality, with some politicians dismissing its credibility. While embedded evaluators are seen as a step toward transparency, experts argue they lack teeth without federal mandates. California Governor Gavin Newsom recently issued an executive order to accelerate audit requirements, but Trump’s administration has blocked federal AI-safety reporting. The plan faces skepticism as AI leaders, long opposed to regulation, now propose self-policing measures that may not address systemic risks.

item.title: 5 Takeaways From The Times’s Re-Examination of the O.J. Simpson Case
item.description:
Source: The New York Times
New evidence from unsealed records suggests O.J. Simpson may have had an accomplice in the 1994 murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman. The New York Times obtained documents revealing Joseph Ippolito, a convicted drug trafficker and mafia associate, provided critical information to federal investigators about the case. Ippolito, who escaped prison a month before the murders, had close ties to Simpson’s friend Al Cowlings and allegedly knew details about Simpson’s alleged domestic violence, drug use, and efforts to evade justice. Prosecutors noted Ippolito’s insights into the disposal of the murder weapon, though the weapon was never found. Ippolito’s brother, Sam, told the Times that Joey Ippolito helped discard a bag containing a heavy object after the murders, though he later recanted under pressure from a documentary producer. Simpson’s 2007 book described a hypothetical accomplice who helped dispose of evidence, but prosecutors dismissed the account. Despite Ippolito’s cooperation, the information arrived too late for the 1995 trial, where he was never called as a witness. The Los Angeles Police Department’s cold case unit continues to investigate, with a spokesman stating the case remains open due to the lack of a conviction. Simpson was civilly liable for the deaths and died in 2024.

item.title: The world is facing an almighty LNG crunch
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics
Qatar's LNG supply disruptions have created a global crisis, with Europe facing potential winter shortages. The Gulf state, once a reliable supplier, has delivered just 98 cargoes in the past year, missing 536 shipments and causing a 39m-tonne shortfall—9% of global supply. LNG prices in Asia are 140% higher than pre-war levels at $25 per mmBtu. While Europe has secured alternatives from the U.S., Australia, and Nigeria, its gas storage is at 73% capacity, the lowest on record for this time of year. Forecasters warn a cold winter could trigger a rush to secure supplies, potentially pushing prices to $30-40 per mmBtu. A severe winter could see prices soar further, with analysts noting that any grid issues, like empty hydro reservoirs or nuclear shutdowns, could exacerbate the crisis. Qatar has not restarted its liquefaction plants, signaling no near-term relief. Europe may need an additional 20m tonnes of LNG by next winter, risking further price hikes. Meanwhile, new LNG projects in the U.S., Canada, and emerging markets could boost global supply to 630m tonnes by 2030, potentially creating a 55m-75m-tonne surplus. This could drive prices below $6 per mmBtu, below long-term contract costs. Market participants are adopting flexible strategies, including trading desks and storage assets, to navigate volatility. However, the transition to surplus could lead to stranded cargo and market instability for years.

item.title: Decoupling From the U.S. Is Awkward
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic
Canada is accelerating military modernization amid rising security threats and strained relations with the U.S. Since 1957, Canada has relied heavily on U.S. military cooperation through NORAD, allowing it to contribute to joint defense at lower cost. Former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau’s government invested billions in U.S.-made equipment, including F-35 fighter jets and surveillance planes. However, Donald Trump’s presidency shifted Canadian strategy, with his rhetoric about annexing Canada and trade wars prompting concerns over U.S. intentions. Trudeau warned Trump sought Canada’s economic collapse, leading his successor, Mark Carney, to increase defense spending to 2% of GDP by 2035 and explore alternatives to U.S. equipment. Carney’s government plans to route 70% of defense contracts to Canadian firms by 2035, diversify partnerships with Europe and the Pacific, and replace some U.S.-made systems with Swedish alternatives. Despite these efforts, Canada remains reliant on U.S. infrastructure for communication, intelligence, and command networks. Challenges include funding shortfalls, limited domestic defense industry capacity, and the need for long-term contracts. The U.S. suspended a joint continental defense board after Carney criticized the global rules-based order, highlighting tensions over military cooperation. While Canada maintains operational ties with the U.S., its leaders acknowledge the risks of overdependence and aim to balance self-reliance with continued collaboration. Mounting threats from China and Russia complicate decoupling, though most military leaders expect the U.S.-Canada relationship to stabilize after Trump’s term ends.

item.title: Tax Systems Unprepared for AI-Driven Fiscal Crisis
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Leaders Original headline: A hurricane is coming to tax systems
Tax systems in the rich world face an impending crisis as artificial intelligence disrupts labor markets and challenges traditional revenue models. Rising borrowing costs in France and Germany, along with the UK’s fiscal challenges, highlight the strain on public finances. Tax structures, reliant on labor income, are increasingly vulnerable to AI-driven shifts that could displace workers or depress wages while boosting corporate profits. Examples include Germany’s VAT disparity on oat milk versus cow’s milk, which creates fiscal inefficiencies, and Britain’s punitive tax changes that force high earners to cut hours or overfund pensions. OECD nations currently collect only 58% of potential revenue from consumption taxes due to exemptions. Unfairness persists, with median employees paying 55% more in taxes than self-employed counterparts. Proposals like California’s wealth tax on billionaires face administrative hurdles, as past attempts failed. Experts warn that a 10-point drop in labor’s share of GDP could double Italy’s budget deficit and strain Germany and France. AI could also generate new tax-avoidance strategies, outpacing governments’ ability to adapt. Solutions include taxing wealth via capital gains, simplifying tax codes, and reducing labor taxes to ease employment costs. Without reform, the fiscal impact of AI could worsen, demanding urgent action to prevent deeper crises.

item.title: AI-Driven Growth Fuels Markets But Risks Economic Fragility
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: The Powerful Yet Fragile Force Propping Up Stocks and the Economy
AI-driven tech stocks have fueled a surge in the stock market and U.S. economic growth, but the reliance on artificial intelligence is raising concerns about stability. The iShares U.S. Technology ETF, tracking AI-led tech stocks, returned 35.2% this year, compared to 4.4% for the broader S&P 500 excluding tech. Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, estimated AI contributed 0.6 to 0.7 percentage points to GDP growth in the second quarter, potentially accounting for 30% of inflation-adjusted economic expansion. However, the reliance on AI is fragile. Evan Hubinger, an Anthropic safety researcher, warned the chance AI could 'kill all humans' within a decade exceeds 10%, prompting calls for regulatory 'guardrails' to slow development. President Trump dismissed such concerns as a 'hoax,' fearing an AI slowdown could trigger a stock market crash and recession. Analysts warn the AI-driven stock boom may be a bubble, with Capital Economics predicting the AI equity market boom is nearing its end. Rising bond yields and energy prices are testing global stock market resilience. While corporate profits remain strong, the concentration of the S&P 500 in tech stocks—now dominated by AI firms like Nvidia, Apple, and Microsoft—poses risks. A collapse in AI stocks could harm retirement funds and the broader economy, which relies on AI for the 'wealth effect' and infrastructure spending. Goldman Sachs estimates global AI-related capital expenditures will reach $1 trillion by 2026, while Columbia University’s Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh projects U.S. AI capital spending could hit $10.3 trillion by 2032, surpassing past infrastructure booms. Higher bond yields, however, could strain AI projects, complicating the economic benefits. The AI boom’s long-term impact remains uncertain, balancing potential productivity gains with job displacement risks.

item.title: Fed Struggles to Measure Inflation Amid Methodological Challenges
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: How the Fed should measure inflation
The Federal Reserve faces challenges in accurately measuring inflation, echoing past struggles of 1970s chairman Arthur Burns. Burns sought to isolate 'underlying' inflation by excluding volatile categories like energy and food, but his approach faced criticism for oversimplification. Today, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has revived this debate, dismissing traditional core inflation indices as a 'rough swag' and advocating for trimmed averages that exclude extreme price swings. Warsh argues that current measures, such as the core PCE index, fail to capture broader inflation trends, citing examples like the 2021 surge where trimmed measures understated inflation. Economists like Jim Dolmas and Evan Koenig of the Dallas Fed note that core indices exclude some volatile items while retaining others, creating inconsistencies. Alternative methods, such as median CPI calculations and trimmed-mean PCE, aim to smooth out idiosyncratic price movements but risk misrepresenting inflation if price patterns shift. The Dallas Fed’s trimmed-mean PCE, which historically dropped more price declines than increases, struggled during the 2021 inflation spike and has since adjusted its methodology. Warsh supports real-time data initiatives like the Billion Prices Project to improve accuracy but acknowledges that no method perfectly captures underlying inflation. He emphasizes focusing on the 'middle' of price distributions, though critics warn that median measures can miss significant trends if a minority of prices surge. The Fed’s quest for a reliable inflation metric remains unresolved, balancing the need for simplicity with the risk of excluding genuine inflationary pressures.

item.title: AI Uses Employee Emails to Train Models, Sparks Legal Disputes
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: You’re not sending an email. You’re training a model
AI note-takers are collecting employee communications to train machine-learning models, sparking legal disputes over data privacy. Google’s $10 million bid to acquire Spirit Airlines’ data—including 100 million emails and 500 million Teams messages—has drawn challenges from rival bidder Micro1, software firm Springshot, and a union representing flight attendants. The union argues the deal includes confidential employee data. Legal experts note that European privacy laws like GDPR restrict reusing data for purposes beyond its original intent, complicating AI training with employee correspondence. A 2017 European Court of Human Rights ruling reinforced employee privacy rights, rejecting an employer’s claim to access an employee’s personal instant-messaging conversations. In the U.S., where data laws are more permissive, companies face other risks: AI transcripts expand discoverable material in litigation. Employees increasingly resist workplace monitoring, as seen with Meta’s failed attempt to track keystrokes, which triggered internal backlash. Legal scholars warn that AI’s use of internal data will make employees more guarded, shifting workplace communication toward professionalism and reducing personal interactions. The trend could reshape how employees balance private and professional messaging, with potential long-term impacts on corporate culture.

item.title: Governments Shift to Stricter Policies to Combat Obesity
item.description:
Source: The Economist - International Original headline: Nagging people to eat healthily does not work
Governments are shifting from persuasion to strict policies to combat rising obesity. Colombia’s 10% tax on unhealthy foods, which rose to 15% in 2024 and 20% in 2025, and mandatory warning labels on processed products have shown measurable impact. Similar measures include California’s law requiring grocery stores to place healthy foods in high-traffic areas and Scotland’s ban on prominent displays of unhealthy items. India is considering restricting junk food sales near schools, while Maharashtra already prohibits such sales within 50 meters of schools. Past efforts to curb obesity through awareness campaigns and limited restrictions failed, with England’s obesity rate doubling since the 1990s and 72% of U.S. adults now classified as obese or overweight. Labeling initiatives, like France’s proposed mandatory traffic-light ratings and Singapore’s labeling requirements, aim to guide consumer choices. Mexico’s 2020 labeling law reduced calories and sugar in products by 15% and 25%, respectively, through reformulation. Restrictions on marketing unhealthy foods are expanding, with Britain and Portugal banning online and social media ads for such products. Enforcement challenges persist, as businesses often find workarounds, such as moving unhealthy items to exempt areas like fresh produce sections. Some governments are exploring alternative approaches, like setting minimum healthiness targets for supermarket sales, which could incentivize retailers to reformulate products. Taxing junk food remains a popular strategy, with over 100 countries imposing levies on sugary drinks, including Mexico’s recent tax hike. Public support for stricter regulations is growing, with 51% of Americans and 70% of Britons favoring expanded taxes and restrictions if funds are used to promote healthier diets.

item.title: French Teen Maimed by Tear Gas Grenade During School Unrest
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: The French Teen Maimed During School Unrest by Tear Gas Grenade
A 14-year-old French boy, Eden, suffered severe facial injuries after a tear gas grenade was fired at him by a police officer during a confrontation at a school in a Parisian suburb. According to prosecutors, video footage and witness accounts, the incident unfolded when officers attempted to disperse students during unrest. A male officer shoved Eden with a tear gas launcher, a female officer struck him with a baton, and Eden kicked at the female officer before the male officer fired a grenade at his face, breaking his jaw and destroying his teeth. Eden, who has not been able to speak since surgery, is facing long-term medical complications. The officer involved has been suspended and investigated, though he claimed he acted to protect his team. The incident sparked national outrage, contributing to widespread protests and riots in France. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu criticized the contradictory police approach, calling it a 'French kind of schizophrenia.' The protests, initially about school conditions, escalated into nationwide unrest, with police accused of both underreacting and using excessive force. Prosecutors are investigating 34 cases of police misconduct, including injuries from stun grenades and rubber bullets. Eden’s mother, fearing retribution, has asked prosecutors to consider charging the officer with attempted murder. The incident highlights ongoing tensions over police tactics during protests, with experts criticizing the use of heavy weaponry against minors. Eden’s case underscores the broader debate over state violence and the impact of police actions on student-led demonstrations.

item.title: Russian Woman's Death Sparks Plague Speculation Amid Lab Links
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Original headline: What We Really Know About the Russian ‘Plague’ Case
A woman who died in a Siberian hospital from pneumonia of unknown cause has sparked speculation about a potential plague outbreak linked to her work at a research facility. Russian authorities have provided limited details, prompting theories about lab-related contamination. Officials confirmed she was a technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, but did not disclose her identity. Local officials placed 200 people under medical observation after reports of contact with an individual who may have had an 'especially dangerous infection.' However, Russian health agencies stated no pathogens linked to her work were found in her samples, and no contacts showed symptoms. The case has fueled concerns about lab accidents or bioweapons, citing Russia's history of secrecy around biological threats, including a 1979 anthrax outbreak linked to a military facility. Scientists emphasize that pneumonic plague, the only form transmissible between humans, requires close contact and has a short incubation period. Experts like David Wagner and Amesh Adalja note the low likelihood of a large outbreak, as plague is treatable with antibiotics. The U.S. State Department and CDC are monitoring the situation, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio downplaying risks but urging Russia for transparency. While some compare the incident to early pandemic fears, experts stress pneumonic plague differs significantly from COVID-19 in transmission and threat level. The Russian government's opaque response has amplified speculation, though no evidence supports claims of a lab-modified pathogen or bioterrorist activity.

item.title: Airfares Rise 24% Amid Spirit Airlines Exit and Fuel Costs
item.description:
Source: NYT > Your Money Original headline: Airfares Have Spiked. Is the Death of Spirit Airlines to Blame?
Airfares have surged by 24 percent in August 2025 compared to the previous year, with domestic Thanksgiving fares rising 31 percent. Economists attribute the spike to factors like fuel costs, inflation, and reduced competition from budget carriers. Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy in May 2025 removed a key price pressure, contributing to fare increases on its former routes. Cirium data shows median fares on 1,126 Spirit routes rose 25.3 percent in the year after the airline's closure, with some routes seeing over 40 percent hikes. Destinations like Detroit, Houston, and Las Vegas saw significant price jumps, with Detroit fares rising from $125 to $227. The impact extended beyond Spirit’s network, with median fare increases of 18.3 percent on routes without Spirit service. Analysts note overlapping pressures including fuel, labor costs, and strong summer demand without sufficient seat additions. Remaining low-cost carriers like Frontier and Allegiant charge fees for extras, while hybrid carriers like JetBlue and smaller airlines like Breeze Airways offer alternatives. Legacy carriers now offer basic economy tickets with limited flexibility. Tips for finding cheaper fares include booking during off-peak days, using flexible travel dates, and checking fare windows. Experts recommend prioritizing routes with lower demand and leveraging points or credits for savings.

item.title: United’s C.E.O. Says It Should Cost More Not to Sit in the Middle Seat
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business
Scott Kirby, CEO of United Airlines, argues that charging more for middle seats is necessary to fund improved travel experiences. He defended his stance during an interview, emphasizing that airlines must cover rising costs like fuel and technology upgrades. Kirby, who took over United during the pandemic, highlighted investments in free Starlink internet, seat-back entertainment, and a user-friendly app to reduce traveler stress. He dismissed claims that rising fares disadvantage frequent fliers, stating that prices are still lower than pre-pandemic levels when adjusted for inflation. Kirby also endorsed a national wealth tax and inheritance taxes, calling wealth inequality a societal threat. His management style focuses on leadership over compliance, prioritizing strategic decisions over daily operations. Kirby shared personal insights, including his upbringing in Texas, his role as a father of seven, and his use of AI as a tutor to learn programming. He criticized common AI applications as 'ridiculous,' advocating for its use in solving complex problems rather than superficial tasks. Kirby also addressed his past dismissal from American Airlines, calling it a 'betrayal' but crediting the experience with shaping his leadership approach. He stressed the importance of personal accountability in overcoming professional setbacks and emphasized efficiency in work-life balance, balancing family time with rigorous routines.

item.title: Sulphur shortage disrupts global markets as war strains supply chains
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: A shortage of sulphur could hurt mines and farms everywhere
A shortage of sulphur is disrupting global markets, impacting mines, farms, and industries reliant on the chemical. The crisis stems from refinery shutdowns in the Gulf and Russia due to the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes, reducing sulphur production. Russia cut exports from 4.8m tonnes in 2025 to 1.8m tonnes in 2026, while Houthi attacks and American tariffs further strained supplies. Middle Eastern sulphur prices surged to $500 a tonne in February 2026, up from $340 a year earlier. The Hormuz Strait closure trapped 25% of global sulphur production, and shipments remain 2/3 below pre-war levels. Non-Gulf exports are 40% lower than before the conflict. China’s ban on acid exports, which previously accounted for 40% of global sulphur trade, has reduced demand, though prices briefly exceeded $1,000 a tonne. Chipmakers are least affected, but copper and nickel miners face challenges. Phosphate fertilizer producers, which require large amounts of sulphur, cut output in 2026, with Mosaic calling it the worst shortage since 2008. Indonesia’s sulphur purchases dropped 75%, and miners delayed maintenance. New capacity in China and India won’t alleviate the crisis soon. Amba Coombe of Argus Media notes sulphur is now viewed as a strategic commodity, not just a by-product, as the Iran war expands the list of critical resources.

item.title: Dollar strengthens amid euro weakness and U.S. economic growth
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: The bond market sell-off is helping the dollar
The dollar has strengthened despite earlier predictions of weakness, driven by factors like the euro's decline, rising French bond yields, and U.S. energy exports. The DXY index rose 4% in 2026, reaching its highest level since 2025. The euro fell to $1.12 from $1.17 as European political and fiscal concerns grew, while French 10-year bond yields climbed to 4.9% from 3.5%. Higher oil prices from U.S.-Iran tensions also benefit the dollar, as America now exports energy rather than imports it. Strong U.S. economic growth—2.5% in Q1 and 2.2% in Q2—has fueled demand for American assets. The Federal Reserve’s interest rate hikes have made U.S. Treasury bonds and corporate debt more attractive, with foreign buyers purchasing $450 billion in corporate debt and $900 billion in stocks in 2026. However, the dollar’s strength is narrower than historical periods, where its appeal relied on both domestic growth and global crises. Analysts warn that if U.S. risk assets underperform, investors may quickly shift away from the dollar, leading to greater volatility. The dollar’s current rally reflects a mix of safe-haven demand and appetite for American assets, but its sustainability depends on ongoing economic and geopolitical factors.

item.title: Medicare Advantage 2027 Plan Finder Improves but Still Has Limitations
item.description:
Source: The New York Times Original headline: Choosing a Medicare Advantage Provider for 2027 May Be Easier, but Not Perfect
Medicare Advantage plan changes for 2027 include improved tools for finding providers but still pose risks for beneficiaries. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services upgraded the Medicare Plan Finder tool to allow searches by any licensed health care provider, not just doctors, and display up to 15 addresses per physician due to location-specific network participation. Annual open enrollment begins Thursday, with a Dec. 7 deadline to choose a 2027 plan or switch to traditional Medicare. However, over 5 million beneficiaries may face coverage gaps due to plan cancellations by UnitedHealthcare and Humana, which will discontinue nearly a million plans. Most affected UnitedHealthcare members will have access to other plans, while Humana did not comment. Critics note that Advantage plans can alter benefits, costs, and service areas annually, and network changes often occur without notice. For example, Blythe Carey received a $963 bill after her gynecologist left her plan’s network, and Mary Ann Davis faced a $1,906 charge after her periodontist’s network changed. Medicare Advantage plans must cover all traditional Medicare services but offer extra benefits like dental and vision. Insurers receive $615 billion in subsidies this year, 14% more than traditional Medicare. A KFF study found Advantage plans cover about half as many doctors as traditional Medicare in 2022. The Plan Finder tool, while improved, still lacks details on provider contract end dates or availability of new patients. Advocates like the American Hospital Association urge CMS to allow plan switches if network information is inaccurate, but this option will not be available for 2027. Experts warn beneficiaries should verify provider details directly, as insurers may not approve long-term care even if a facility is in-network. CMS plans to require insurers to update provider directories every 90 days and remove outdated entries within five business days. Critics argue the burden of verifying coverage falls on patients, with Ms. Carey stating, 'Why is the onus on the patient?' and Ms. Davis noting the frustration of 'all that work... didn’t do me any good.'

item.title: The Economist seeks paid foreign desk interns
item.description:
Source: The Economist - International Original headline: Paid interns on The Economist’s foreign desk
The Economist is offering paid internships for foreign affairs writers. The positions are based in London and require applicants to have the right to work in the UK. Interns will serve for six months and must submit three article ideas as part of their application. Two of these ideas should include short pitches proposing potential stories for publication, while the third must be a completed 600-word article suitable for The Economist. Applicants must also provide a CV and cover letter. The deadline for applications is October 30, 2026. The internship aims to identify future journalists, with no prior experience required. Applicants are prohibited from using AI to generate pitches or finished articles, though AI tools may be used for research purposes. The Economist emphasizes diversity and equal opportunities, welcoming candidates of all backgrounds. All submitted work must be original, with the pitches and completed article being the most critical components of the application.

item.title: America's Financial Revolution Drives Record Deals and AI Investments
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: The era of speedball capitalism has dawned
American financial markets are undergoing a rapid transformation marked by record-breaking deals and investments. In the past year, the U.S. has seen the largest initial public offering (SpaceX), equity raise (Google), foreign firm bond issue (SK Hynix), private-funding round (OpenAI), and private-debt deal (Broadcom). Amazon completed the biggest bond issue in history, while mergers in railways, utilities, and media—such as Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery—led to the largest junk-bond offering. New markets for compute and predictions have emerged, overshadowing concerns about corporate scandals and hedge-fund failures. The financial system blurs traditional boundaries between state and market, public and private, and investment and gambling. Companies like Nvidia, now the world’s most valuable firm, operate as venture-capital investors and lenders. Goldman Sachs and Apollo have evolved into asset managers and hybrid insurers, respectively. The U.S. economy’s focus on maintaining AI leadership over China has driven massive spending commitments, with tech giants like Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft allocating $2.4trn to data-center projects. A study by Columbia Business School projects that 183GW of new data-center capacity by 2032 could surpass the scale of past railway and dotcom booms. Spillovers affect industries like gas turbines and utilities, while banks profit from financing data centers. Household net worth has reached 830% of disposable income, reflecting the market’s dominance. The system’s risks include pressure on life-insurance markets, Oracle’s force majeure claims for data-center projects, and delayed listings like Oura’s due to market uncertainty. The global economy envies America’s capital machine, which has spread Wall Street practices like private equity and debt restructuring abroad. The system’s fragility is underscored by questions about what might break, as risks accumulate despite record highs in stock markets and bond yields.

item.title: The Blog Post That Set the AI World on Fire
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology
AI researcher Nick Cammarata's 26,000-word blog post has ignited intense debate in Silicon Valley. The document challenges the prevailing belief that generative AI models are inscrutable black boxes, arguing instead that their inner workings can be understood. Cammarata, a former OpenAI employee now at Goodfire, claims neural networks have self-consistent functions, using examples like neurons responding to V-shaped patterns. This would make AI systems predictable rather than mysterious, potentially enabling safer control over the technology. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and researcher Adam Majmudar praised the work, calling it a major breakthrough. However, critics like Google DeepMind's Neel Nanda argue the findings don't address how networks function as a whole, comparing it to understanding atoms without predicting weather. The post, labeled a 'working hypothesis' for an upcoming paper, focuses on vision models rather than complex language models like ChatGPT. Skeptics note the lack of peer review and the blog's technical limitations. While some see the research as a path to safer AI, others warn against overestimating its implications, highlighting the industry's history of unfulfilled promises. The debate underscores tensions between optimism about AI transparency and concerns over corporate accountability in an unregulated field.

item.title: Stripe acquires AI model marketplace OpenRouter for $7.5 billion
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Business Original headline: The rise of the AI marketplace
Businesses are struggling with unpredictable AI token costs, spurring the growth of model marketplaces. OpenRouter, co-founded by Alex Atallah in 2023, allows companies to switch between AI models to manage expenses. The platform charges a fee for routing traffic and has attracted major interest, with Stripe acquiring it for $7.5 billion in August. OpenRouter competes with cloud providers like Amazon and Google, which offer their own models but face skepticism for potential bias. The marketplace enables users to test models and prioritize cost-effective options, with cheaper systems from Chinese firms like DeepSeek and Z.ai dominating token usage. Atallah argues many companies fail to optimize token spending by categorizing tasks into low, medium, and high 'entropy' levels. He advises using affordable models for routine tasks and reserving advanced models for complex work. 'The mistake I see a lot of companies make is they just don’t decompose all of these things. It is all the same to them,' Atallah said, calling this approach a 'massive waste of money.'

item.title: Vladimir Putin and the pariah problem
item.description:
Source: The Economist - International
German officials blamed Russia for a failed drone attack on a Leipzig airport, marking a shift from previous diplomatic caution. French President Emmanuel Macron warned Russia’s hybrid attacks would 'not go unanswered,' while European leaders debated balancing condemnation of Putin’s actions with the need for peace. The G20 summit in December, hosted by Donald Trump, will include Putin and Ukraine’s Zelensky, raising concerns about diplomatic engagement. Analysts at the Helsinki Security Forum warned that Russia’s war crimes may never face justice, with Russian elites refusing reparations and war criminals possibly holding political power. Ukraine’s allies emphasize the need to deny Putin a 'full-throated victory' to prevent further aggression, while acknowledging the war’s stalemate may require uneasy coexistence. Despite global condemnation, Putin retains allies, including Trump, China, and India, complicating efforts to isolate him. European leaders face a dilemma: framing the conflict as a moral crusade against a rogue state risks political gains for populists, yet failing to condemn Russia’s actions could embolden its aggression.

item.title: Europe's Cities Are Pleasant but Lack Economic Power
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Europe Original headline: Europe has lots of pleasant cities but too few that matter
Europe's cities are known for their charm but lack the economic scale of global metropolises. Paris, the EU's largest city with nearly 10 million residents, trails behind New York in economic output and Shanghai in population. The EU's top 10 urban areas account for just 16% of the bloc's economic output, compared to 33% in the U.S. and 15% in China and India. The OECD notes that doubling a city's population is linked to double-digit productivity growth, yet Europe's urban landscape remains fragmented. Historical factors, including weak central governance and municipal independence, shaped Europe's dense network of midsize cities. Despite EU integration, no city has emerged as a global powerhouse like New York or Shenzhen. This dispersion harms competitiveness in industries like AI, where talent gravitates toward hubs like San Francisco. While some argue connecting nearby cities could create a regional megacity, practical barriers like cross-border logistics and diminishing returns on proximity limit this. Europe's model of numerous pleasant cities avoids the extremes of sprawling 'flyover country' but risks falling behind in global economic races.

item.title: Tech Holdouts Resist Upgrades, Embrace Simplicity and Control
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Technology Original headline: The Upgrade Holdouts
Tech holdouts resist upgrading their devices, embracing simplicity, cost savings, and control over their digital lives. These users, ranging from older adults to minimalists, reject the fast-paced tech cycle by clinging to older gadgets like 2003 iPods, Bush-era computers, and decade-old smartphones. Mike Tyran, a 66-year-old nurse, uses a 2003 iPod now displayed in a museum and calls himself 'Old Turkey' on tech repair site iFixit. Gary Flanagan, a 54-year-old nonprofit consultant, relies on a legacy 3G network with his iPhone 5S, despite limited app access. Others, like Larye Parkins, cite practicality: 'I’m just cheap.' The trend challenges planned obsolescence, a practice where companies design products to shorten lifespans. Apple faced lawsuits over slowing older iPhones and restricting third-party repairs. Holdouts face hurdles like phased-out networks, software incompatibilities, and e-waste concerns. Some find workarounds, such as using Linux to revive old computers or jailbreaking Kindles. Communities like iFixit host repair events, while projects like Rebble revive discontinued smartwatches. Despite challenges, many holdouts prefer the autonomy of outdated tech over modern complexities. However, some, like Tyran, face pressure to upgrade due to family or technical limitations. For now, they remain defiant, choosing inconvenience over the relentless pace of technological advancement.

item.title: Human Brain Evolution Linked to Alzheimer’s Risk
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: The Evolution of the Human Brain Set It Up for Failure
Human brain evolution may have increased susceptibility to Alzheimer’s disease. Apes do not develop the condition like humans do, despite sharing significant DNA. Researchers compare human and primate brains to identify genetic and structural differences linked to Alzheimer’s. Melissa Edler’s team found distinct patterns in amyloid plaque and tau tangle accumulation between humans and chimpanzees.
